summary: A patriotic lyric figuring the American nation as a woman whose triple-suit gown, cut at Lexington, still defies Great Britain's disapproval with its bayonet.

title: 1515. The Things that never can come back, are several —
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditative lyric on irrecoverable losses (Childhood, Hope, the Dead), contrasting travelers who return with the spirit's one-way journey to its Native Land.

title: 1519. The Dandelion's pallid tube
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric in which the dandelion's bud and shouting flower proclaim, like a resurrection, that winter's sepulture is over.

title: 152. The Sun kept stooping — stooping — low!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A sunset rendered as a martial pageant of Tyrian color and armies that vanish at the chimney corner; nature, light and imagination.

title: 1521. The Butterfly upon the Sky,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric praising the homeless, nameless, tax-free butterfly as a model of freedom; soaring without sighing is offered as the way to grieve.

title: 1524. A faded Boy — in sallow Clothes
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac pastoral lyric on a dead farm boy (a statesman's embryo) and his cow, now remanded to oblivion, a ballad's barn and clover's retrospect.

title: 1525. He lived the Life of Ambush
author: Dickinson
summary: An epitaphic lyric for a secretive man who died into dusk, his name now marked by an asterisk/star in which the whole of immortality lies entrenched.

title: 1526. His oriental heresies
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful nature lyric of the bee's gay apostasy across earth and air, finally lured to die upon the lowly clover where butterflies expire.

title: 1527. Oh give it Motion — deck it sweet
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a corpse, begging it be given motion and words, betrothed again to that Pink stranger Dust it now knows more intimately than the living.

title: 1528. The Moon upon her fluent Route
author: Dickinson
summary: A cosmological lyric in which moon and stars (the Star's Etruscan Argument) substantiate a God, yet the knowing astral ones are forgotten as Dawn forgets them.

title: 1529. 'Tis Seasons since the Dimpled War
author: Dickinson
cluster: Lust / Sexual Desire · Desire · Sin and the Fall
summary: A lyric figuring love as a mutual war in which both lovers were conqueror and slain, fought without formula, each the other's Pink Redoubt.

title: 153. Dust is the only Secret —
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling personification of Death as a secretive stranger who, like a bird, has its nest robbed by Christ; mortality, dust and faith.

title: 1530. A Pang is more conspicuous in Spring
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on grief sharpened by spring's renewal; the contrast of singing things makes loss conspicuous, and even Resurrection had to wait till they moved a Stone.

title: 1532. From all the Jails the Boys and Girls
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of children's release from the prison of school into a beloved afternoon of solid bliss, shadowed by Frowns lying in wait for such joy.

title: 1533. On that specific Pillow
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the threshold of sleep and death, where projects flit away and the soul can do no more than try to comprise the night's tremendous morrow.

title: 1535. The Life that tied too tight escapes
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric using the runaway horse as emblem of a constrained life that, once it escapes, runs forever wary, and is shot down if recaptured.

title: 154. Except to Heaven, she is nought.
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy for a humble woman likened to an unnoticed flower, yet whose loss empties a home; grief, humility and the value of the small.

title: 1540. As imperceptibly as Grief
author: Dickinson
summary: A celebrated lyric on the imperceptible lapse of summer, likened to grief, as the season makes her light, wingless escape into the Beautiful.

title: 1542. Come show thy Durham Breast
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric addressed to a robin, inviting it to display its breast and make its minute nuptial avowal within the speaker's tree before soaring away.

title: 1545. The Bible is an antique Volume —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: A satirical lyric recasting Scripture's cast as literary characters and concluding that a warbling teller like Orpheus would win all the Boys where condemnation fails.

title: 1547. Hope is a subtle Glutton —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wine and Drink · Food and Feasting · The Inn / Tavern
summary: An epigrammatic lyric personifying Hope as a glutton who feeds on the Fair yet practices abstinence, dining alone at a Halcyon Table where nothing is diminished.

title: 1549. My Wars are laid away in Books —
author: Dickinson
summary: A late lyric on facing one last Battle against an unseen Foe (Death), hoping not to be forgotten by the chums and playmates already passed away.

title: 155. The Murmur of a Bee
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on nature's inexpressible witchcraft — bee, hill, dawn — that cannot be explained, only attributed to the divine Artist; wonder and inexpressibility.

title: 1551. Those — dying then,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the loss of faith: the dying once knew their destination, but now God's Right Hand is amputated; better an ignis fatuus than no illumination.

title: 1554. "Go tell it" — What a Message —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on dutiful obedience unto death, invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae who gave their dying kiss to Law rather than to longing or endearment.

title: 1555. I groped for him before I knew
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of solemn, nameless spiritual hunger for a foreshadowed, consecrated Food (Christ/the divine) that others spurn but the speaker reveres as the only Food that grows.

title: 1558. Of Death I try to think like this —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric reimagining death's grave as a beckoning brook and a Hesperian flower beyond, recalling a childhood leap to clutch a purple flower despite the roaring water.

title: 156. You love me — you are sure —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A love lyric anxiously seeking reassurance against abandonment and the sting of betrayal; romantic love, doubt and fear of loss.

title: 1560. To be forgot by thee
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric of unrequited love and memory: to be forgotten by the beloved surpasses all other minds' remembrance; being worthy to be forgot is the speaker's renown.

title: 1561. No Brigadier throughout the Year
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric celebrating the Jay as a civic warrior braving winter winds, intimate with snow, and protesting that immortality would be unfair to leave this neighbor out.

title: 1562. Her Losses make our Gains ashamed —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric praising a woman who bore Life's empty Pack gallantly; the heaviest burden is emptiness, and to punish honey only makes it sweeter.

title: 1568. To see her is a Picture —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of devoted love and friendship: to see, hear and know her is picture, tune and innocent intemperance, while to lack her is affliction and to own her sunlit warmth.

title: 157. Musicians wrestle everywhere —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a mysterious, omnipresent celestial music — the spheres, the morning stars, the blessed dead; wonder, faith and the inexpressible.

title: 1570. Forever honored by the Tree
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric honoring an apple tree visited by two robins figured as Gabriels/angels, registered in Nature's Book yet modestly screened from renown.

title: 1573. To the bright east she flies,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of a departed soul flown eastward to Paradise, remitted home by its Brothers; the living, dreaming, find existence strays homeless at home.

title: 1574. No ladder needs the bird but skies
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the bird's effortless freedom needing no ladder or grim baton, linking its few implements of bliss to Jesus's invitation 'Come unto me.'

title: 1575. The Bat is dun, with wrinkled Wings —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric riddle on the inscrutable, songless bat, an 'Elate Philosopher' of mysterious origin, whose eccentricities the speaker ascribes to a beneficent Creator.

title: 1576. The Spirit lasts — but in what mode —
author: Dickinson
summary: A metaphysical lyric probing the relation of spirit and body (music and violin, tides and sea) and whether consciousness persists after death, met by a shut Rumor's Gate.

title: 1579. It would not know if it were spurned,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the safety of the insentient flower that cannot feel rejection, yet may despair that it is no Cavalier free to dare and perish in love.

title: 158. Dying! Dying in the night!
author: Dickinson
summary: A dramatic deathbed cry for light and for Jesus, comforted at last by a beloved's arrival; death, faith, doubt and consolation.

title: 1581. The farthest Thunder that I heard
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on a transformative bolt of lightning that struck the speaker alone; the obligation to that electric, waylaying Light founds the homes and explains life's reverberation.

title: 1584. Expanse cannot be lost —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric on a death that opens an infinite expanse; the world shuts for the departed, but the following troops are gone and only the listening Tent remains.

title: 1585. The Bird her punctual music brings
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the bird's faithful song laid in the human heart and heavenly grace, where Beauty's tireless toil becomes electric rest for those who make magic.

title: 1586. To her derided Home
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A summer weed blooms in a despised home then departs like a lady; closes on Christ's invitation and the few 'Codes of Bliss.' Nature and grace woven together.

title: 1587. He ate and drank the precious Words —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: A reader feeds on words/books, gaining spiritual robustness and liberty; celebration of the redemptive, immortalizing power of literature.

title: 1588. This Me — that walks and works — must die,
author: Dickinson
summary: Certainty of personal death sealed before birth; meditation on mortality and the fixed fate of the self.

title: 1589. Cosmopolities without a plea
author: Dickinson
summary: Wandering birds as world-citizens bearing 'compliments of Paradise'; their roving theology is 'Knock and it shall be opened.'

title: 159. A little bread — a crust — a crumb —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric praising a modest sufficient life over ambition, invoking Napoleon and soldiers; humility, contentment and the worth of little.

title: 1591. The Bobolink is gone —
author: Dickinson
summary: The departed bobolink as a rowdy, irreverent preacher disrupting the 'Presbyterian Birds'; gentle satire of solemn piety through nature.

title: 1593. There came a Wind like a Bugle —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A sudden apocalyptic storm sweeps the world yet it abides; the sublime terror of nature's catastrophic force.

title: 1597. 'Tis not the swaying frame we miss,
author: Dickinson
summary: Grief over the dead: it is the steadfast loving heart, not the body, we mourn; love endures through the tomb.

title: 1598. Who is it seeks my Pillow Nights —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: Conscience as a nightly inquisitor and childhood nurse interrogating the speaker over guilt and judgment.

title: 160. Just lost, when I was saved!
author: Dickinson
summary: A near-death narrative of returning from the threshold of eternity with untellable secrets; mortality, immortality and the afterlife.

title: 1600. Upon his Saddle sprung a Bird
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird's free flight and lavished song that strikes the listening universe; the artist/songster and the power of the lyric note.

title: 1601. Of God we ask one favor,
author: Dickinson
summary: We ask forgiveness for a hidden crime while immured in life's 'magic Prison,' reprimanded for happiness; doubt and theological paradox.

title: 1603. The going from a world we know
author: Dickinson
summary: Dying as a child's lonely climb toward an unknown hill of sorcery; uncertainty whether the secret of death compensates.

title: 1604. We send the Wave to find the Wave —
author: Dickinson
summary: A divine errand sent wave to wave, the messenger lost in love; the futility of wise distinctions made too late.

title: 1606. Quite empty, quite at rest,
author: Dickinson
summary: A robin, nest emptied of lost young, sets out homeless on faith for 'rumored Springs'; bereavement and resilient hope in nature.

title: 161. A feather from the Whippoorwill
author: Dickinson
summary: A jeweled emblem-lyric of an everlasting singing bird whose nest the ages spin; nature, song and the eternal in the natural world.

title: 1612. The Auctioneer of Parting
author: Dickinson
summary: Death/parting personified as an auctioneer crying 'going, going, gone' from the Crucifix, selling wilderness and despair; loss and Christ's death.

title: 1617. To try to speak, and miss the way
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Stammering, tearful gratitude as a ragged poverty; the irrepressible 'Mutineer' Soul that words cannot conceal — on inexpressibility.

title: 1624. Apparently with no surprise
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Frost beheads a flower as a 'blonde Assassin' while the Sun and an approving God proceed unmoved; nature's casual cruelty and theodicy.

title: 1626. No Life can pompless pass away —
author: Dickinson
summary: Every death, lowliest or exalted, joins the same funeral pageant; the democratic mystery and miracle of mortality.

title: 1628. A Drunkard cannot meet a Cork
author: Dickinson
summary: A winter fly triggers intoxicating memory; the speaker is a connoisseur of delight whose true liquor is joy taken from the bee.

title: 163. Tho' my destiny be Fustian —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric preferring a humble 'gypsy' lot to fine damask, since both bloom eternally beyond frost and autumn; humility, immortality and transience.

title: 1630. As from the earth the light Balloon
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul like a balloon longs for ascension/release, indignant at the dust that bound it; the spirit's yearning for immortality.

title: 1631. Oh Future! thou secreted peace
author: Dickinson
summary: The Future as a hunter's den that inexorably takes its 'sacred Prey'; no cunning route of grace can balk fate.

title: 1632. So give me back to Death —
author: Dickinson
summary: Bereaved of the beloved, the speaker breathes in her own grave; loss makes death welcome and measures heaven and hell by it.

title: 1633. Still own thee — still thou art
author: Dickinson
summary: Watching a loved one slip toward a 'reportless Grave,' desperate for a last answer before death takes them into the 'recallless sea.'

title: 1634. Talk not to me of Summer Trees
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: The mind's inner foliage as a tabernacle for incorporeal birds; imagination and the spiritual realms beyond physical nature.

title: 1635. The Jay his Castanet has struck
author: Dickinson
summary: The jay's castanet and the cricket's 'sable line' announce winter's close of swarthy autumn days; seasonal change in nature.

title: 164. Mama never forgets her birds,
author: Dickinson
summary: A consolation lyric: a dead mother, like God noticing fallen sparrows, still tends her children from above; grief, providence and faith.

title: 1640. Take all away from me, but leave me Ecstasy,
author: Dickinson
summary: Ecstasy alone makes the speaker richer than all; yet a guilty awareness of those in abject poverty at the door.

title: 1642. "Red Sea," indeed! Talk not to me
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Defiant boast of a sunset 'Navy in the West' outshining Pharaoh's Red Sea; the divine glory of a sky overwhelming the eye, exultation amid woe.

title: 1643. Extol thee — could I? Then I will
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Praising the heavenly beloved: perceiving and partaking of the loved one is evidence of the sky and a guaranty of immortality. Love as religion.

title: 1645. The Ditch is dear to the Drunken man
author: Dickinson
summary: The drunkard's ditch as bed and sanctuary under the sky, oblivion bending over him while honor lies far off; intoxication and the outcast.

title: 1646. Why should we hurry — why indeed?
author: Dickinson
summary: No escape from the molesting inference of immortality; uncertainty about life's begun labors besets sight in the 'mighty night.'

title: 1649. A Cap of Lead across the sky
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A leaden, face-hiding storm-sky chills noon into a well, combining the charms of winter and hell; nature's sublime menace and God withdrawn.

title: 165. A wounded Deer — leaps highest —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Deception · Short Story
summary: A lyric arguing that extreme suffering produces the highest response and that mirth masks anguish; pain, concealment and the psychology of suffering.

title: 1650. A lane of Yellow led the eye
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A painterly sunset of yellow and purple wood whose hidden inhabitants and the truth of the scene remain impossible to know; nature and the unknowable.

title: 1651. A Word made Flesh is seldom
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: Language as eucharist and incarnation: a word made flesh has power not to die; reverent meditation on the immortal, sacramental power of the word.

title: 1652. Advance is Life's condition
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave is only a relay, not a terminus; an unlit tunnel of continued existence preferable to non-existence. Mortality and immortality.

title: 1655. Conferring with myself
author: Dickinson
summary: Beside a wandering bird the speaker's cares and whole career seem paltry and superfluous; nature's freedom shaming human anxiety.

title: 1656. Down Time's quaint stream
author: Dickinson
summary: Life as a forced, oarless voyage down Time's stream toward a secret port, no surety from wind or tide; the journey of life toward death.

title: 1657. Eden is that old-fashioned House
author: Dickinson
summary: Paradise is the ordinary home we inhabit unawares until we leave it irrecoverably; nostalgia, the fall from innocence, paradise lost.

title: 1659. Fame is a fickle food
author: Dickinson
summary: Fame as fickle food on a shifting plate that crows scorn; 'Men eat of it and die' — satire of glory's transience. Sic transit gloria.

title: 166. I met a King this afternoon!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: A whimsical narrative finding hidden royalty in a barefoot country boy; humility, the common man and the inversion of worldly rank.

title: 1663. His mind of man, a secret makes
author: Dickinson
summary: Each mind carries an impregnable circumference, a secret unknowable even to the neighborly other; the inviolable solitude of the self.

title: 1664. I did not reach Thee
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: A long allegorical journey of rivers, deserts and seas to reach the beloved, with Death finally usurping the prize; love as quest toward the unattainable.

title: 1665. I know of people in the Grave
author: Dickinson
summary: The dead would prize the smallest news; remembrance of them expands the least event and the mere right to walk the earth.

title: 167. To learn the Transport by the Pain
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on learning joy through deprivation and exile, the suffering becoming inaudible laureates; pain, longing and the artist's woe.

title: 168. If the foolish, call them "flowers" —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric setting flowers and faith above science, glimpsing a Mosaic landscape of heaven; faith, nature and humility before mystery.

title: 169. In Ebon Box, when years have flown
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on keepsakes in a black box — letters, a pressed flower, a curl — that revive memory of the dead; memory, transience and nostalgia.

title: 17. Baffled for just a day or two —
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief lyric on encountering Spring as an 'unexpected Maid' in the garden whose nod awakens the woods; wonder at nature's renewal.

title: 171. Wait till the Majesty of Death
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on death ennobling the lowly clay into royal state, leveling rank under the Lord of Lords; mortality, the common man and faith.

title: 172. 'Tis so much joy! 'Tis so much joy!
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of joy gambled against failure, weighing life, death and the overwhelming prospect of heaven; joy, mortality and faith.

title: 1727. If ever the lid gets off my head
author: Dickinson
cluster: The World Upside Down · Madness · Madness
summary: Whimsical conceit of the brain escaping the skull, probing the relation of sense, soul, and identity.

title: 173. A fuzzy fellow, without feet,
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddle-lyric tracing the caterpillar's seasonal metamorphosis into the butterfly; nature, seasons and transformation as secret.

title: 1731. Love can do all but raise the Dead
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Love's near-omnipotence stops at death; it tires and sleeps, abetting the departing fleet of the lost.

title: 1732. My life closed twice before its close —
author: Dickinson
summary: Bereavements as life-closings; parting equated with both heaven and hell, meditating on immortality.

title: 1733. No man saw awe, nor to his house
author: Dickinson
summary: The sublime terror of confronting divine awe, glossed by Moses seeing God face to face.

title: 1736. Proud of my broken heart, since thou didst break it,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: Suffering of love rendered through Christ's Passion, crucifixion and cup of anguish; love as religion.

title: 1737. Rearrange a "Wife's" affection!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: A secret, suffering devotion figured as martyrdom, thorns and a hidden diadem borne until death.

title: 1738. Softened by Time's consummate plush,
author: Dickinson
summary: Time softens childhood griefs that now seem easy beside bleaker adult despair; memory and mutability.

title: 1739. Some say goodnight — at night —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Parting equated with night and presence with dawn; a private code of farewell and light imagery.

title: 1740. Sweet is the swamp with its secrets,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: Nature's charm spoiled by a snake; summer's treason recalls the Edenic fall from innocence.

title: 1741. That it will never come again
author: Dickinson
summary: Transience itself makes life sweet; the paradox that finitude rather than belief instigates desire.

title: 1742. The distance that the dead have gone
author: Dickinson
summary: The slow realization of the dead's distance and our own following them through grief and memory.

title: 1743. The grave my little cottage is,
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave domesticated as a cottage where the speaker keeps house awaiting reunion in everlasting life.

title: 1744. The joy that has no stem no core,
author: Dickinson
summary: An intangible joy, edible to longing but not to display, prized precisely for its imperviousness.

title: 1746. The most important population
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: The unnoticed nations of bumble-bees in the grass possess a heaven without hell; nature's hidden order.

title: 1747. The parasol is the umbrella's daughter,
author: Dickinson
summary: Playful epigram personifying parasol and umbrella as frivolous daughter and honored father.

title: 1748. The reticent volcano keeps
author: Dickinson
summary: Nature's reticent volcano keeps the secret Jehovah told her; the one secret kept is immortality.

title: 1749. The waters chased him as he fled,
author: Dickinson
summary: A drowning narrative; the sea-billow lures the fleeing man toward a revolting bliss of death by water.

title: 175. I have never seen "Volcanoes" —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Deception · Short Story
summary: A lyric likening the still human face to a volcano hiding titanic anguish that may erupt; suppressed suffering, concealment and the sublime.

title: 1751. There comes an hour when begging stops,
author: Dickinson
summary: Prayer abandoned as vain; a flat refusal kinder than a disappointing God's deferral. Doubt and faith.

title: 1752. This docile one inter
author: Dickinson
summary: Burial of a docile dead one, dauntless in the House of Death; the living arraign life's sunny brevity.

title: 1753. Through those old Grounds of memory,
author: Dickinson
summary: Memory as an intoxicating internal bar, a divine intemperance offering longing without recovery.

title: 1754. To lose thee — sweeter than to gain
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Loss preferred to gain; the Caspian needs its sterile sands, so love needs its drought to be itself.

title: 1756. 'Twas here my summer paused
author: Dickinson
summary: Summer's halt and the removal to winter; seasons figure the loss and parting of love and life.

title: 1757. Upon the gallows hung a wretch,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Justice / Right and Wrong · Revenge · Avenger
summary: An executed outcast, condemned by law, mourned by his mother; the grim ballad of justice and a mother's love.

title: 1759. Which misses most,
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditation on grief weighing the loss of the tending hand and the blessing lip now gone to sleep.

title: 176. I'm the little "Heart's Ease"!
author: Dickinson
summary: A flower's monologue resolving to bloom regardless of weather, allied to an unchanging Eden; nature, constancy and steadfast faith.

title: 1760. Elysium is as far as to
author: Dickinson
summary: Heaven or doom waits in the very nearest room; the soul's fortitude as it awaits a coming footstep.

title: 1761. A train went through a burial gate,
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird sings over a funeral procession in the churchyard, bidding good-bye to men; nature beside death.

title: 1762. Were natural mortal lady
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Nature's unhurried departure contrasted with mortal haste; beauty enchanting more by leaving.

title: 1764. The saddest noise, the sweetest noise,
author: Dickinson
summary: Spring birdsong, sweet and maddening, recalls the dead and the lost; an ear can break the heart like a spear.

title: 1769. The longest day that God appoints
author: Dickinson
summary: A letter-poem of encouragement: even the longest appointed day of anguish finishes with the sun.

title: 1771. How fleet — how indiscreet an one —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A letter-poem on the fleet, indiscreet, always-wrong joyful Deity of Love we are not scourged to serve.

title: 1773. The Summer that we did not prize,
author: Dickinson
summary: The unprized summer instructs by departing; belated recognition chases trains already out of sight.

title: 1775. The earth has many keys,
author: Dickinson
summary: Earth's many musical keys; beauty is nature's fact and the cricket the speaker's utmost elegy.

title: 178. I cautious, scanned my little life —
author: Dickinson
summary: A parable of hoarded 'hay' (the lasting things of life) mysteriously stolen, turning the speaker cynic and questioner; loss, doubt and providence.

title: 179 8 FIRE, FAMINE, AND SLAUGHTER
author: Coleridge
cluster: War and its Cost · Blood · American Civil War
summary: A 'war eclogue' in which the personified hags Fire, Famine and Slaughter, loosed by Pitt over La Vendee and Ireland, gloat over carnage; themes of war's cost, power and corruption, in dramatic verse.

title: 179. If I could bribe them by a Rose
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of the poet-beggar offering flowers and song to win admission, undeterred by storm or death; longing, the artist and devotion.

title: 18. The Gentian weaves her fringes —
author: Dickinson
summary: An autumn-death lyric: the gentian and red maple frame a funeral of summer attended by bobolink and bee, closing in a trinitarian benediction; mortality, nature and faith.

title: 180. As if some little Arctic flower
author: Dickinson
summary: An analogy of an Arctic flower wandering south into summer and Eden, leaving the inference to the reader; nature, wonder and paradise.

title: 181. I lost a World — the other day!
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on losing a precious starry 'world' that the rich overlook but the speaker prizes; loss, grief and the value of the small.

title: 183. I've heard an Organ talk, sometimes
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a cathedral organ working an inexplicable spiritual change on the listener; faith, wonder and the inexpressible sublime.

title: 184. A transport one cannot contain
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on contained ecstasy that, if loosed, would overwhelm the universe; joy, the sublime and the inexpressible.

title: 186. What shall I do — it whimpers so —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A love lyric figuring the restless heart as a whimpering hound (Carlo) offered to the beloved; romantic love, longing and devotion.

title: 187. How many times these low feet staggered —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric meditating on a dead housewife's stilled body and abandoned chores; an emblem of mortality and the silence of the corpse.

title: 188. Make me a picture of the sun —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: A playful lyric of imaginative substitution, conjuring sun, robin and summer through art and make-believe against coming frost.

title: 190. He was weak, and I was strong — then —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric on mutual dependence and parting between two souls, reading as both intimate love and a homeward journey toward death.

title: 191. The Skies can't keep their secret!
author: Dickinson
summary: A whimsical lyric on nature's gossip of spring's coming, ending in reverence for the Father's mystery and the value of not-knowing.

title: 192. Poor little Heart!
author: Dickinson
summary: A tender song to a forsaken heart, consoling it through grief and abandonment with imagery of morning glory, wind and sun.

title: 193. I shall know why — when Time is over —
author: Dickinson
summary: A hymn-meter lyric deferring the explanation of earthly anguish to Christ in heaven, balancing present suffering against eternal understanding.

title: 194. On this long storm the Rainbow rose —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric where storm clears to rainbow and sun, yet one sleeper is dead and only the archangel can wake her; nature versus death.

title: 195. For this — accepted Breath —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric of spiritual election figured as a royal crown and eternal June, with Gabriel and saints proclaiming immortal glory.

title: 196. We don't cry — Tim and I,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A lyric in a child's voice on hidden grief, prayer, and a wish to die simultaneously with a beloved companion.

title: 198. An awful Tempest mashed the air —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric personifying a violent storm as a spectral monster, resolving into morning calm that is called Paradise.

title: 199. I'm "wife" — I've finished that —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A lyric on the transformation from girlhood to wifehood, comparing the change to entering heaven and questioning the contrast of states.

title: 2 HENRY IV
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: A history play of the dying Henry IV and the final maturation of Prince Hal, ending with his accession as Henry V and the cold rejection of Falstaff; pervaded by themes of sickness, mortality, time, and the burden of rule.

title: 2. There is another sky
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature vs Civilization · The Garden · Pastoral Retreat
summary: A lyric inviting her brother into an unfading inner garden immune to frost and faded forests; nature imagery transfigured into a private eternal realm.

title: 20. Distrustful of the Gentian —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of self-reproach and resolve to sing through the coming winter, with mirage-like images (phantom meadow, brooks in deserts) of distant heaven to a hand below.

title: 201. Two swimmers wrestled on the spar —
author: Dickinson
summary: A stark sea lyric of shipwreck: one swimmer survives, one drowns, his dead face still beseeching; survival, death, and divine silence.

title: 203. He forgot — and I — remembered —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric figuring betrayal and remembered fidelity through Peter's denial of Christ at the temple fire; love, guilt, and faith.

title: 204. A slash of Blue —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A painterly lyric composing dawn and evening skies from slashes of color; pure nature-as-art and the sublime spectacle of sky.

title: 205. I should not dare to leave my friend,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of devoted vigil, dreading the friend's deathbed and the heartbreak of arriving too late; loyalty, death, and grief.

title: 206. The Flower must not blame the Bee —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric using the flower-and-bee courtship as a witty figure of romantic pursuit and discreet refusal.

title: 207. Tho' I get home how late — how late —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the ecstasy of a long-deferred homecoming, figuring reunion (or death/heaven) as worth decades of agony.

title: 208. The Rose did caper on her cheek —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric watching a girl's blushing agitation, revealed as mutual love when an answering blush ticks two hearts into one.

title: 213. Did the Harebell loose her girdle
author: Dickinson
summary: A sensuous lyric questioning whether yielding in love preserves or dissolves reverence, via harebell, bee, Paradise and Eden.

title: 214. I taste a liquor never brewed
author: Dickinson
summary: An ecstatic lyric of intoxication on air, dew and summer; a debauchee of nature drinking until seraphs and saints look on.

title: 215. What is — "Paradise" —
author: Dickinson
summary: A child-voiced lyric domesticating heaven, asking homely questions about Eden, the Father, and dying as homesick travel.

title: 216. Safe in their alabaster chambers
author: Dickinson
summary: A major lyric on the dead sleeping in tombs awaiting resurrection while heedless nature and toppling empires roll on overhead.

title: 217. Savior! I've no one else to tell —
author: Dickinson
summary: A prayer-lyric addressed to Christ, bringing him the unbearable, heavier-since-lost heart of love and grief to hold.

title: 218. Is it true, dear Sue?
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A short playful lyric to Sue about a new baby, wishing to bottle the infant up so as to come and see him.

title: 219. She sweeps with many-colored Brooms —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric personifying the sunset as a housewife sweeping the western sky with colored brooms that fade into stars.

title: 22. All these my banners be.
author: Dickinson
summary: A spring-garden lyric where flowers are banners and pageantry, the grave-hillocks built gaily for daisy and columbine; nature, joy and a buried resurrection hope.

title: 221. It can't be "Summer"!
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling lyric puzzling over a season (or death), resolved when a rouge sunset shuts the question with cuffs of chrysolite.

title: 222. When Katie walks, this simple pair accompany her side,
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief affectionate valentine-like lyric on faithful companionship walking and kneeling beside Katie; friendship and devotion.

title: 223. I Came to buy a smile — today —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric offering jewels in a mercantile bargain to purchase a single smile; love figured as commerce and longing.

title: 224. I've nothing else — to bring, You know —
author: Dickinson
summary: A tender lyric on humble repeated gifts, likened to night's faithful fetching of stars that guide one home; love and constancy.

title: 227. Teach Him — When He makes the names —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: An intimate lyric asking that a baby's first babbled names include the speaker's, blending tenderness, prayer and longing.

title: 228. Blazing in Gold and quenching in Purple
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A vivid sunset lyric figuring the sun as a leaping leopard and a juggler of day, blazing and dying into the horizon.

title: 229. A Burdock — clawed my Gown —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on petty injuries from burdock and bog, moralizing that only minnows despise while the elephant looks calmly on.

title: 23. I had a guinea golden —
author: Dickinson
summary: A reproachful lyric on three lost treasures — a gold guinea, a robin, a Pleiad star — as figures for a missing friend; loss, fidelity and the wish for the traitor's remorse.

title: 230. We — Bee and I — live by the quaffing —
author: Dickinson
summary: A bacchic lyric of the bee and poet living by drinking nature's wine, ending found dead of nectar by a humming coroner.

title: 231. God permits industrious Angels —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A lyric in childhood imagery of playing with an angel until God calls him home at sunset; loss, faith, and dreariness after grace.

title: 232. The Sun — just touched the Morning —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: An allegorical lyric of Morning exalted then abandoned by the wheeling Sun-King, left crownless; love, loss, and longing for glory.

title: 233. The Lamp burns sure — within —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the soul's inner lamp burning on even when the careless servant fails to fill it; the self, soul, and light within.

title: 234. You're right — "the way is narrow" —
author: Dickinson
summary: A satirical lyric translating the gospel's narrow way into mercantile terms of price, discount, dividend and jail; faith, doubt, irony.

title: 235. The Court is far away —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric of pleading before an offended Sovereign-King, offering to intercede for him in turn; faith, humility, royal imagery.

title: 236. If He dissolve — then — there is nothing — more —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric of dread at a beloved's failing pulse, figured as eclipse, blindness, and the fading star of Bethlehem; grief, death, faith.

title: 237. I think just how my shape will rise —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric imagining one's resurrected shape rising forgiven in heaven, pleading as the sparrow of God's care; faith, doubt, redemption.

title: 24. There is a morn by men unseen —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A visionary lyric of an unseen otherworldly morn where the dead maids keep a 'seraphic May' in dance and song; immortality, the afterlife and a different dawn.

title: 26. It's all I have to bring today —
author: Dickinson
summary: A dedicatory lyric offering the heart, the fields, the meadows and the bees as a total gift; love, generosity and the whole of nature given over.

title: 27. Morns like these — we parted —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of a beloved's death-and-rising figured as a bird (linnet) parting at morn and flying free at evening; parting, transport and grief.

title: 281. 'Tis so appalling — it exhilarates —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric on the paradoxical relief of confronting death and terror directly; horror becomes exhilaration once suspense and hope are abandoned.

title: 282. How noteless Men, and Pleiads, stand,
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric on sudden disappearance and death, men and stars vanishing into the invisible while heaven sweeps by indifferent.

title: 283. A Mien to move a Queen —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: Portrait lyric of a shy, regal-yet-humble figure, half child half heroine, who inspires reverence; a study of identity and bearing.

title: 284. The Drop, that wrestles in the Sea —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric using the drop-and-ocean conceit for the lover's self-loss into the beloved and the soul's relation to the infinite.

title: 285. The Robin's my Criterion for Tune —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric on provincial perception: nature is measured by one's own New England seasons and birds; identity rooted in place.

title: 286. That after Horror — that 'twas us —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric of near-death terror, a brush with the abyss off a crumbling pier; death personified as a steel-faced figure drilling its welcome.

title: 287. A Clock stopped —
author: Dickinson
summary: Famous death lyric figuring a death as a stopped clock no craft or doctor can restart; mortality, time, and the gulf between life and the dead.

title: 288. I'm Nobody! Who are you?
author: Dickinson
summary: Famous epigrammatic lyric prizing private anonymity over public fame; identity, alienation, and satire of social self-display.

title: 289. I know some lonely Houses off the Road
author: Dickinson
summary: Narrative lyric imagining a burglary of an isolated house at night; a playful gothic of stealth, terror, and the watching moon and stars.

title: 29. If those I loved were lost
author: Dickinson
summary: A terse riddle-lyric on how the speaker would know the fate (lost, found, dead) of those she loves, with bells of Ghent and a Philip allusion; love and loss.

title: 290. Of Bronze — and Blaze —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Lyric on the northern lights' sovereign indifference, contrasting cosmic majesty with the poet's mortality and a brief borrowed arrogance.

title: 291. How the old Mountains drip with Sunset
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Ekphrastic nature lyric painting a sunset as a fiery canvas no Old Master could capture; the sublime and inexpressibility of beauty.

title: 292. If your Nerve, deny you —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric of stoic courage urging the soul to lean against the grave when nerve fails; fortitude in the face of death and despair.

title: 293. I got so I could take his name —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric of gradual recovery from loss, measured by enduring the beloved's name and letters; grief, prayer, doubt, and a remote God.

title: 294. The Doomed — regard the Sunrise
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Lyric contrasting the condemned man's heightened perception of sunrise and birdsong with the joyful's; mortality sharpens beauty into elegy.

title: 295. Unto like Story — Trouble has enticed me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: Lyric drawing courage from martyrs and revolutionaries who suffered for glory; suffering as crucifixion and a martial march toward the light.

title: 296. One Year ago — jots what?
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric of anniversary reckoning with a lost intimacy, growth and grief, the unrecognized wine of love now turned to thirst.

title: 297. It's like the Light —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Definition lyric chasing an ineffable joy through analogies of light, bee, woods, and morning; inexpressibility and wonder.

title: 298. Alone, I cannot be —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: Lyric on never being alone for nameless supernatural hosts that visit and never leave; imagination, the unseen, and inner company.

title: 299. Your Riches — taught me — Poverty
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Love lyric using mines, gems, and treasure of Peru and Golconda to figure the wealth of the beloved and the speaker's bereft poverty.

title: 3. Sic transit gloria mundi
author: Dickinson
summary: A long comic valentine stuffed with Latin tags, schoolroom learning, and patriotic allusions, mock-meditating on mortality, glory and transience.

title: 30. Adrift! A little boat adrift!
author: Dickinson
summary: A sea-allegory contrasting sailors' report of a little boat foundering with angels' report of it retrimming its sails and shooting exultant on; death, the soul and salvation.

title: 300. "Morning" — means "Milking" — to the Farmer —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Definition lyric cataloguing what 'morning' means to farmer, lover, bride, and faith; dawn as relative revelation and divine experiment.

title: 301. I reason, Earth is short —
author: Dickinson
summary: Skeptical syllogistic lyric weighing earth's brevity, inevitable decay, and an uncertain heaven, each undercut by 'but what of that?'; faith and doubt.

title: 302. Like Some Old fashioned Miracle
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric likening summer's memory after its end to a fairy-tale miracle and a silenced orchestra; transience, memory, and nostalgia.

title: 303. The Soul selects her own Society —
author: Dickinson
summary: Famous lyric on the soul's sovereign, absolute choice of one companion and its stone-like exclusion of all else; identity, will, and alienation.

title: 304. The Day came slow — till Five o'clock —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Nature lyric staging sunrise as a jeweled spectacle of rubies and topaz with the wind as prince; wonder and gratitude at dawn.

title: 305. The difference between Despair
author: Dickinson
summary: Definition lyric distinguishing despair from fear as the calm after a wreck; psychic numbness figured as a sightless bust.

title: 306. The Soul's Superior instants
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric on rare visionary instants when the solitary soul ascends to glimpse eternity and immortality; self and soul, the sublime.

title: 307. The One who could repeat the Summer day —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: Lyric exalting the artist who could reproduce a summer day and sunset above nature itself; immortality of art and the imagination.

title: 308. I send Two Sunsets —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: Witty lyric of the poet competing with the day, making two sunsets and stars to its one; art rivaling nature, imagination's craft.

title: 31. Summer for thee, grant I may be
author: Dickinson
summary: A love lyric vowing to be the beloved's everlasting summer and flower, skipping the tomb to bloom forevermore; love, devotion and immortality over death.

title: 310. Give little Anguish —
author: Dickinson
summary: Epigrammatic lyric contrasting noisy small grief with the marble-silent sublimity of death's great anguish; suffering and silence.

title: 311. It sifts from Leaden Sieves —
author: Dickinson
summary: Famous riddle lyric describing snow filling and erasing the landscape like alabaster wool, then vanishing like ghosts; winter, transience, nature.

title: 312. Her — "last Poems" —
author: Dickinson
summary: Elegy for Elizabeth Barrett Browning, the 'Anglo-Florentine', whose silenced song mourns a poet buried in Italy; art, death, and praise.

title: 313. I should have been too glad, I see —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: Lyric arguing that denied joy and defeat sanctify faith, invoking Sabachthani, Calvary, and Gethsemane; suffering, faith, and redemption through loss.

title: 314. Nature — sometimes sears a Sapling —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Lyric comparing nature's wounding of trees with the human soul's more frequent, less fatal deaths; suffering, nature, and resilience.

title: 315. He fumbles at your Soul
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Famous lyric figuring an overwhelming spiritual or aesthetic force as a musician building to a thunderbolt that scalps the soul; the sublime and terror.

title: 316. The Wind didn't come from the Orchard — today —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Playful nature lyric personifying the wind as a transient, mischievous fellow tracked by its scents and havoc; nature and wonder.

title: 317. Just so — Jesus — raps —
author: Dickinson
summary: Lyric imaging Christ patiently knocking at the soul's door; divine love, grace, faith, and the soul awaiting salvation.

title: 318. I'll tell you how the Sun rose —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Nature lyric narrating a vivid sunrise and a mysterious sunset led away by a grey 'Dominie'; wonder, beauty, and gentle faith.

title: 319. The nearest Dream recedes — unrealized —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Disillusionment · Odysseus / Ulysses · Grace Under Pressure / Stoic Endurance
summary: Lyric figuring unattainable desire and heaven as a bee evading a schoolboy; longing, the receding dream, and disillusionment.

title: 32. When Roses cease to bloom, Sir,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric anticipating the speaker's own death (the gathering hand lying idle in Auburn cemetery) once summer's flowers and bees are gone; mortality and transience.

title: 320. We play at Paste —
author: Dickinson
summary: Parable lyric on apprenticeship: practicing on paste prepares the hand for pearl; art, craft, growth, and the value of practice.

title: 321. Of all the Sounds despatched abroad,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Lyric celebrating the wind's music in the boughs as an inalienable inheritance persisting even past death; nature, music, immortality, and joy.

title: 322. There came a Day at Summer's full,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: A lyric recounting a sacred day of union between two souls, figured through Eucharist, marriage and crucifixion imagery; love sanctified as religion, parting endured in hope of resurrection.

title: 323. As if I asked a common Alms,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A brief lyric of overwhelming, unexpected grace: a modest plea answered with a kingdom and a flood of dawn, expressing wonder and gratitude.

title: 324. Some keep the Sabbath going to Church —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A witty lyric/hymn-form poem placing private worship in nature above institutional churchgoing; the book of nature as scripture and personal faith over ritual.

title: 325. Of Tribulation, these are They,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: A lyric on the white-robed victors of suffering (Revelation), reframing earthly defeat and anguish as spiritual triumph and salvation.

title: 326. I cannot dance upon my Toes —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: An ars poetica lyric: the untrained poet claims an inward, unperformed art as full as opera or ballet; on imagination, the artist, and hidden creative power.

title: 327. Before I got my eye put out
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric on sight, loss, and possession: the speaker, deprived of eyes, contemplates the overwhelming sublimity of owning all nature and retreats to safer inner vision.

title: 328. A Bird came down the Walk —
author: Dickinson
summary: A close observational nature lyric of a bird's feeding and startled flight, moving from raw realism to a sublime image of effortless beauty in motion.

title: 329. So glad we are — a Stranger'd deem
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on the near-identity of grief and joy, so alike that even an optician could not tell them apart.

title: 33. If recollecting were forgetting,
author: Dickinson
summary: A paradox-lyric inverting remembering/forgetting and grief/joy to convey how deeply the speaker remembers and mourns; memory, loss and paradox.

title: 332. There are two Ripenings — one — of sight —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compact nature lyric contrasting two kinds of ripening — visible fruit and the hidden burr disclosed only by autumn frost — emblem of maturation and time.

title: 333. The Grass so little has to do —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature vs Civilization · The Garden · Pastoral Retreat
summary: A pastoral lyric idealizing the grass's simple, humble life, even its sweet death into hay, ending in a wish for such untroubled being.

title: 334. All the letters I can write
author: Dickinson
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: A sensuous miniature comparing writing to a flower's velvet depths sipped by a hummingbird; on desire, beauty, and the inexpressible in words.

title: 335. 'Tis not that Dying hurts us so —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric arguing that living hurts more than dying, figuring the dying as migrating birds and the living as those who stay to suffer winter.

title: 336. The face I carry with me — last —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric in which the beloved's face becomes the speaker's rank and crown beyond death; love as religion, with angelic coronation and heavenly royalty.

title: 337. I know a place where Summer strives
author: Dickinson
summary: A seasonal nature lyric personifying Summer's losing struggle against Frost, with the south wind reviving her vow; on mutability and cyclic seasons.

title: 338. I know that He exists.
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of faith shadowed by doubt: God's hiddenness as playful ambush, with a dread that the game may turn deadly earnest; faith, doubt, and death.

title: 339. I tend my flowers for thee —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lush garden lyric of longing for an absent beloved, the blooming flowers offered to the absent lord; on desire, fidelity, and unrequited love.

title: 34. Garland for Queens, may be —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A brief lyric distinguishing garlands and laurels for queens and heroes from the humble rose Nature ordains in charity and equity; humility, nature and remembrance.

title: 340. Is Bliss then, such Abyss,
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: A playful lyric weighing the irreplaceable, once-sold bliss against a replaceable boot, resolving to risk all for joy; on desire and choice.

title: 341. After great pain, a formal feeling comes —
author: Dickinson
summary: A major lyric on the numb, mechanical aftermath of suffering, likened to freezing to death; on grief, the formal feeling of trauma, and psychic deadness.

title: 342. It will be Summer — eventually.
author: Dickinson
summary: A seasonal lyric prophesying summer's return to a snow-bound village, its flowers and bees figured in sacramental terms; on cyclic renewal.

title: 343. My Reward for Being, was This.
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric exalting a single bliss/grace above all earthly thrones and realms, sealed by the ballots of eternity; on election, value, and the divine reward.

title: 344. 'Twas the old — road — through pain —
author: Dickinson
summary: A narrative lyric tracing a woman's last journey of suffering to her grave, her relics left behind; on death, the road through pain, and bereavement.

title: 345. Funny — to be a Century —
author: Dickinson
summary: A witty lyric personifying a Century as a discreet, secret-keeping observer of passing humanity; on time, memory, and the silence of history.

title: 346. Not probable — The barest Chance —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the razor-thin margin between salvation and loss, figured by a far-journeying bird who forgets its wing and perishes a bough from Paradise; on fate and grace.

title: 347. When Night is almost done —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A short dawn lyric on the near approach of sunrise dissolving night's terror into trivial memory; on hope, light and dark, and overcome fear.

title: 348. I dreaded that first Robin, so,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of spring's painful return to a grieving speaker who, as Queen of Calvary, salutes the indifferent birds and flowers; on grief, spring, and suffering.

title: 349. I had the Glory — that will do —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compact lyric on possessing a supreme glory that outweighs lesser fames and consumes time's possibilities; on honor, bliss, and value.

title: 35. Nobody knows this little Rose —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a plucked little rose, mourned only by bee, butterfly, bird and breeze; the ease of small, unnoticed deaths and the rose as pilgrim.

title: 350. They leave us with the Infinite.
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a vast, more-than-human God whose mountainous hand upholds the faithful into eternity; on faith, providence, and the sublime.

title: 351. I felt my life with both my hands
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of self-examination in which the speaker tests her existence and identity before a mirror, courageously embracing change; on self, soul, and identity.

title: 352. Perhaps I asked too large —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: An epigrammatic lyric claiming a cosmic largeness of desire — skies and firmaments easy to hold, small bundles hard; on imagination and aspiration.

title: 353. A happy lip — breaks sudden —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Deception · Short Story
summary: A lyric distinguishing spontaneous joy from a patient, gilded merriment that masks pain from unqualified observers; on appearance versus reality and concealed grief.

title: 354. From Cocoon forth a Butterfly
author: Dickinson
summary: A nature lyric of a butterfly's idle, purposeless summer wandering above laboring men, all extinguished at sundown; on transience, idleness, and mortality.

title: 355. 'Tis Opposites — entice —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Lust / Sexual Desire · Desire · Sin and the Fall
summary: An epigrammatic lyric on how lack and deprivation intensify longing — the blind prize sight, the captive freedom; on desire, paradox, and want.

title: 356. The Day that I was crowned
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: A lyric of inward coronation transforming an ordinary day, with the grace of being chosen surpassing the crown itself; on identity, grace, and election.

title: 357. God is a distant — stately Lover —
author: Dickinson
summary: A witty lyric figuring God's vicarious courtship of the soul through Christ via the Miles Standish/Priscilla/John Alden tale; on love divine and faith.

title: 358. If any sink, assure that this, now standing —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · The Battlefield · Horse
summary: A consolatory lyric using battlefield imagery — the whizzing ball, the silence of being hit — to argue the worst is easy in a moment; on death, courage, and heroism.

title: 359. I gained it so —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of a hard-climbed bliss clutched in fear of loss, the speaker dreading return to the contented beggar's poverty; on desire, grace, and the quest.

title: 36. Snow flakes.
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful winter lyric of counting dancing snowflakes ('rebels') until the speaker's own toes join the jig; joy, whimsy and nature.

title: 360. Death sets a Thing significant
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric on how death invests the dead's small relics — needlework, a marked book — with unbearable significance; on death, memory, and grief.

title: 362. It struck me — every Day —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of recurring, lightning-like anguish that nature has lost the date of and left burning in the sky; on suffering, storm imagery, and unending pain.

title: 363. I went to thank Her —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric: the speaker crosses the sea to thank one now dead and asleep in the grave, the return journey heavy with loss; on death, grief, and the grave.

title: 364. The Morning after Woe —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on nature's cruel jubilance the morning after sorrow, its birdsong falling like litanies of lead on the grieving; on grief, dawn, and nature's indifference.

title: 365. Dare you see a Soul at the White Heat?
author: Dickinson
summary: The blacksmith's forge becomes a symbol for the soul's inner refinement through suffering toward a transfigured 'Designated Light'.

title: 366. Although I put away his life —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A renounced beloved is served in devotion that outlasts death, carrying earthly love into Paradise.

title: 367. Over and over, like a Tune —
author: Dickinson
summary: Recollection replays like music, evoking martial cornets of Paradise and the justified at the Lord's right hand.

title: 368. How sick — to wait — in any place — but thine —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Fierce romantic fidelity figured through ships, ports and stormy seas, preferring shared tossing to a mooring without the beloved.

title: 369. She lay as if at play
author: Dickinson
summary: A dead child is depicted as if merely sleeping mid-play, death softened into deep light slumber.

title: 37. Before the ice is in the pools —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric of expectant wonder before winter's coming, hinting at an imminent visitation (death or the unseen) just 'a bridge away'; faith, mystery and transience.

title: 370. Heaven is so far of the Mind
author: Dickinson
summary: Heaven is internalized as a function of mind and capacity, near or infinitely far according to desire.

title: 371. A precious — mouldering pleasure — 'tis —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: An antique book becomes a venerable living interlocutor conjuring Plato, Sophocles, Sappho and Dante across the centuries.

title: 372. I know lives, I could miss
author: Dickinson
summary: Measures the relative weight of lives: a precious few whose loss would be eternity against the many easily outgrown.

title: 373. I'm saying every day
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: Rehearses an imagined elevation to queenship, dressing rustic self for the court against sudden reversals of rank.

title: 374. I went to Heaven —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Imagination · Creativity and Artistic Labor · The One Life (Pantheism)
summary: Heaven imagined as a tiny still ruby-lit town of gossamer society, beautiful as pictures no man drew.

title: 375. The Angle of a Landscape —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: The view framed through a window crack changes with the seasons, fixed chimney and hill contrasted with mutable foliage.

title: 376. Of Course — I prayed —
author: Dickinson
summary: Bitter doubt of an indifferent God who ignores prayer, wishing the oblivion of the atom's tomb over conscious misery.

title: 377. To lose one's faith — surpass
author: Dickinson
summary: Lost faith is irreplaceable unlike a depleted estate; annihilating one clause beggars one's being.

title: 378. I saw no Way — The Heavens were stitched —
author: Dickinson
summary: Cosmic vertigo and alienation as the universe slides away and the self becomes a lone speck on circumference beyond the bell.

title: 379. Rehearsal to Ourselves
author: Dickinson
summary: Rehearsing a withdrawn delight is a self-wounding bliss 'like Murder', cherishing the dirk that commemorates inner death.

title: 380. There is a flower that Bees prefer —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: The clover flourishes as a brave 'Purple Democrat' contending for sun and sod until cancelled by the frost.

title: 382. For Death — or rather
author: Dickinson
summary: Death weighed as a transaction buying room, escape and a name, its gifts incommensurable with life's because the rates lie here.

title: 383. Exhilaration — is within —
author: Dickinson
summary: Inner exhilaration figured as a self-brewed wine more intoxicating than any outer Rhine, kept for sacrament.

title: 384. No Rack can torture me —
author: Dickinson
summary: The soul's liberty defies all bodily torture; the only true captivity is consciousness of being one's own enemy.

title: 385. Smiling back from Coronation
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: The triumph of crowning is shadowed by recognizing former equals left in 'Being's Peasantry', the contrast breeding misery.

title: 386. Answer July —
author: Dickinson
summary: A seasonal catechism passes a question down July, May, the Jay and back to the Year, dramatizing the cycle of the seasons.

title: 387. The sweetest Heresy received
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Mutual love between man and woman is cast as a private religion, each the other's convert in a faith of two.

title: 388. Take your Heaven further on —
author: Dickinson
summary: Addresses one too late for a dying soul dressed in white, urging the visitor to apologize to the skies and move on.

title: 389. There's been a Death, in the Opposite House,
author: Dickinson
summary: A small-town death observed through its social ritual: doctor, minister, undertaker and the coming dark funeral parade.

title: 39. It did not surprise me —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a bird (birdling) leaving the nest for gayer boughs, turning to the dread of a beloved's death — a 'coffin in the heart'; loss and grief.

title: 390. It's coming — the postponeless Creature —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death personified as an inexorable visitor that gains the door, salutes, dresses the house in crape and carries one off to God.

title: 391. A Visitor in Marl —
author: Dickinson
summary: Frost personified as a nocturnal visitor whose caress kills the flowers it touches, annihilating them as if they never were.

title: 392. Through the Dark Sod — as Education —
author: Dickinson
summary: The lily rises in faith through dark soil to ecstatic bloom, an emblem of growth and trust in resurrection.

title: 393. Did Our Best Moment last —
author: Dickinson
summary: Transcendent moments are rationed divine grants that, lasting, would supersede Heaven, then withdraw leaving the soul unfurnished.

title: 394. 'Twas Love — not me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A guilty plea over loving 'most', invoking Christ's death and the confusion of doubles before justice — strike Love, not me.

title: 395. Reverse cannot befall
author: Dickinson
summary: Interior prosperity is invulnerable to misfortune, like a diamond in Bolivian ground that no implement can mar.

title: 396. There is a Languor of the Life
author: Dickinson
summary: A numb languor succeeding extreme pain, a fog obliterating consciousness that even the surgeon recognizes as approaching death.

title: 397. When Diamonds are a Legend,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: The poet's flowers/art outlast vanished diamonds and diadems, patronized once by a Queen and once by a Butterfly.

title: 398. I had not minded — Walls —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Gross barriers could be tunnelled, but the thinnest filament-veil between lovers proves an impassable citadel guarded by dragons.

title: 399. A House upon the Height —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: An unreachable house on the height, untouched by wagon or death, holds an empty pane and a fate only conjecture and God know.

title: 4. On this wondrous sea
author: Dickinson
summary: A short sea-voyage lyric in which the pilot guides the soul across stormy waters to the peaceful shore of Eternity; death as safe harbour.

title: 40. When I count the seeds
author: Dickinson
summary: A faith-lyric on seeds sown beneath and the lowly dead raised high, a 'garden mortal shall not see' picked by faith; resurrection, immortality and the resignation of summer.

title: 400. A Tongue — to tell Him I am true!
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: An urgent message of fidelity to be carried at any price in gold, diamonds and rubies, the bond binding past the world's end.

title: 401. What Soft — Cherubic Creatures —
author: Dickinson
summary: A satire of genteel ladies whose refined 'Dimity Convictions' shrink from human nature and shame even Deity and Redemption.

title: 403. The Winters are so short —
author: Dickinson
summary: Restless seasonal interruptions of summer, ending in the legends of a Deluge and Noah's Ararat that no one credits now.

title: 404. How many Flowers fail in Wood —
author: Dickinson
summary: Unseen flowers perish unconscious of their own beauty, an emblem of unwitnessed worth and obscure fading.

title: 405. It might be lonelier
author: Dickinson
summary: The speaker clings to accustomed loneliness and suffering, fearing that hope would blaspheme a room ordained to pain.

title: 406. Some — Work for Immortality —
author: Dickinson
summary: Contrasts working for the slow everlasting gold of immortality with the immediate currency of fame and time.

title: 408. Unit, like Death, for Whom?
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave as a strict, solitary destination admitting only the dead; meditates on death's silence and the fear of uncertainty.

title: 409. They dropped like Flakes —
author: Dickinson
summary: Mass death (soldiers) imaged as falling flakes and petals; consoled by God's remembrance of every face.

title: 41. I robbed the Woods —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric of guilt at despoiling the trusting woods of their burs and mosses, anxiously wondering what hemlock and oak will say; nature, guilt and trespass.

title: 410. The first Day's Night had come —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The World Upside Down · Madness · Madness
summary: A psyche enduring trauma until the soul's instrument snaps and the brain laughs uncontrollably; questions whether this is madness.

title: 411. The Color of the Grave is Green —
author: Dickinson
summary: The grave's outer colors (green, white) across seasons versus an inner color no snow or summer alters; on memory and loss.

title: 412. I read my sentence — steadily —
author: Dickinson
summary: A death sentence read calmly, the soul made familiar with extremity so it meets Death tranquilly as a friend.

title: 413. I never felt at Home — Below —-
author: Dickinson
summary: Wry confession of alienation from both world and Paradise, with an irreverent God surveilling through a telescope; faith and doubt.

title: 414. 'Twas like a Maelstrom, with a notch,
author: Dickinson
summary: Extended nightmare of psychic torture by maelstrom and goblin, reprieved at the brink; horror and the agony of perishing or living.

title: 415. Sunset at Night — is natural —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: Reversal of natural order (sunset at dawn, midnight at noon) as a challenge to providence and Jehovah's watch.

title: 416. A Murmur in the Trees — to note —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Faint supernatural perceptions in nature (tiny men, robins with wings) the speaker promises never to fully tell; wonder and the inexpressible.

title: 417. Is it dead — Find it —
author: Dickinson
summary: Fragmentary interrogation of the dead's state (happy, conscious, homesick) which the grave cannot answer; on death's silence.

title: 418. Not in this World to see his face —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Earthly life as a mere primer or A-B-C book, content with limited knowledge while the beloved keeps the skies; faith and renunciation.

title: 419. We grow accustomed to the Dark —
author: Dickinson
summary: Adjusting to literal and inner darkness ('Evenings of the Brain') as a parable of endurance through grief and uncertainty.

title: 42. A Day! Help! Help! Another Day!
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric figuring an ordinary day as a battlefield where victory hangs on the soul's steadiness; militant imagery of inner struggle and endurance.

title: 420. You'll know it — as you know 'tis Noon —
author: Dickinson
summary: Mightiest things (God, glory) known by intuition not terms, omnipotence speaking through lightning and sun; faith and the sublime.

title: 421. A Charm invests a face
author: Dickinson
cluster: Appearance vs Reality · Deception · Short Story
summary: The veiled face whose charm depends on imperfect sight; desire sustained by withholding, on appearance versus reality.

title: 422. More Life — went out — when He went
author: Dickinson
summary: The disproportionate vital fire of one who died, requiring extreme cold to quench; grief, loss and the measure of a life.

title: 423. The Months have ends — the Years — a knot —
author: Dickinson
summary: Time as an unbreakable skein of misery; the Earth tenderly laying tired lives to ultimate repose like weary children.

title: 424. Removed from Accident of Loss
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: Unconscious of one's spiritual riches like a Malay diver unaware of pearls he gathers; on hidden worth and the Orient.

title: 425. Good Morning — Midnight —
author: Dickinson
summary: Rejected by Day, the speaker greets Midnight as home; a poignant address on belonging, despair and consolation.

title: 426. It don't sound so terrible — quite — as it did —
author: Dickinson
summary: Rehearsing and reframing the word 'Dead' to make the tomb's terror smaller by habit; on mortality and the mind's defenses.

title: 427. I'll clutch — and clutch —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: Grasping at diamonds and stars to hoard into diadems and display at court; on ambition, wealth and acquisitive desire.

title: 428. Taking up the fair Ideal,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: Idols cast down at their flaw (Adam scowling at Eden) yet cherished till transfigured and mended; on the fall and redemption of the ideal.

title: 429. The Moon is distant from the Sea —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: The moon leading the obedient tide as an emblem of the speaker's submission to a beloved's command; love and devotion.

title: 43. Could live — did live —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric praising one who lived and died in serene faith, contemplating death's journey with unpuzzled heart; faith, death and the soul's voyage.

title: 430. It would never be Common — more — I said —
author: Dickinson
summary: Ecstatic transformation and dowering of the world with joy, then sudden collapse into beggary; rapture and loss.

title: 431. Me — come! My dazzled face
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: Astonished humility at being welcomed and named among the saints in a shining place; on grace and heavenly recognition.

title: 432. Do People moulder equally,
author: Dickinson
summary: Questioning bodily decay against Jesus's promise that some shall not taste death; faith, doubt and immortality.

title: 433. Knows how to forget!
author: Dickinson
summary: A frustrated quest to learn the art of forgetting through school, books, planets and rabbis; memory, grief and impossibility.

title: 435. Much Madness is divinest Sense —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The World Upside Down · Madness · Madness
summary: Aphoristic inversion of madness and sense, with the dissenting individual chained by the conforming majority; on madness and society.

title: 436. The Wind — tapped like a tired Man —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: The wind personified as a footless guest who taps, enters, makes music and departs; a whimsical nature fantasy.

title: 437. Prayer is the little implement
author: Dickinson
summary: Prayer defined as a small apparatus for flinging speech toward God where presence is denied; faith and doubt about being heard.

title: 438. Forget! The lady with the Amulet
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A pledge of constancy figured through the lady, bee, rose and rill that outlasts death; fidelity, love and devotion.
