cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: A lyric on inner conscience: the soul's accusation outweighs all external blame, and its disdain for worldly artifice becomes the truest friendship. Themes: conscience, self and soul, integrity.

title: 754. My Life had stood — a Loaded Gun —
author: Dickinson
summary: Dickinson's enigmatic masterpiece: the speaker as a loaded gun claimed and wielded by a Master/Owner, exploring agency, power, lethal force, and the paradox of power to kill without power to die. Themes: power, identity, self and soul, the riddle of mortality and service.

title: 755. No Bobolink — reverse His Singing
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the bobolink who keeps singing even when his tree is felled and his future cut off, music his only anodyne. Themes: resilience, loss, song as solace, dispossession.

title: 756. One Blessing had I than the rest
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a single supreme blessing so satisfying it becomes a paralyzing bliss, an earthly heaven obscuring judgment. Themes: joy, satisfaction, earthly paradise, the limits of bliss.

title: 757. The Mountains — grow unnoticed —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A nature lyric celebrating the mountains' quiet, unapplauded grandeur and the sun's golden fellowship with their eternal faces. Themes: nature, sublimity, humble grandeur, the natural order.

title: 758. These — saw Visions —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric tenderly addressing the eyes, mouth, and hands of a dead woman now received into Paradise. Themes: death, grief and loss, the body, the dead beloved.

title: 759. He fought like those Who've nought to lose —
author: Dickinson
cluster: War and its Cost · Blood · American Civil War
summary: A war lyric on a soldier who courts death recklessly yet is left alive because death is coy of those who crave it. Themes: war and its cost, death-wish, the paradox of survival, despair.

title: 76. Exultation is the going
author: Dickinson
summary: The inland soul's ecstatic launch into the sea of eternity; the sea as death/immortality and the divine intoxication of release.

title: 760. Most she touched me by her muteness —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric in which a mute, winged beggar from the sky pleads for a crumb of charity, then ascends giving gratitude. Themes: charity, humility, the sacred in the small, gratitude.

title: 761. From Blank to Blank —
author: Dickinson
summary: A bleak lyric of mechanical, aimless trudging through a threadless, blank existence where stopping, perishing, or advancing are indifferent. Themes: despair, alienation, blindness as relief, the journey to nowhere.

title: 762. The Whole of it came not at once —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on protracted suffering as 'murder by degrees,' likened to a cat toying with a mouse; quick death preferred to dying half and rallying. Themes: suffering, mortality, cruelty of prolonged pain.

title: 763. He told a homely tale
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A lyric portrait of a prematurely aged orphan child, scarred and motherless, redeemed alive by the speaker's ransom. Themes: childhood, orphanhood, grief and loss, redemption.

title: 764. Presentiment — is that long Shadow — on the Lawn —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A famous epigrammatic lyric defining presentiment as the long shadow warning grass that darkness is about to fall. Themes: foreboding, transience, intuition of death, nature as omen.

title: 766. My Faith is larger than the Hills —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A devotional lyric in which the speaker's faith outlasts the hills and even steers the sun, becoming the rivet that holds the firmament. Themes: faith, providence, the natural order, cosmic dependence.

title: 767. To offer brave assistance
author: Dickinson
summary: A gnomic lyric distinguishing human from divine charity: to aid the solitary and nameless, whose benediction none stopped to earn, is divine. Themes: charity, humility, the common man, the divine in compassion.

title: 768. When I hoped, I recollect
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric mapping the emotional weather of hope, fear, and despair onto remembered places and seasons, with nature mirroring inner cold and darkness. Themes: hope and despair, memory, melancholy, nature as mirror of the soul.

title: 769. One and One — are One —
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic lyric rejecting school arithmetic for the soul's stark minor choosing among Life, Death, or the Everlasting. Themes: mortality, immortality, the soul's ultimate alternatives, paradox.

title: 77. I never hear the word "escape"
author: Dickinson
cluster: Desire · Value and Scarcity · Gems / Jewels
summary: The word 'escape' and images of prisons broken stir a longing for freedom that repeatedly fails; confinement, liberty and frustrated desire.

title: 770. I lived on Dread —
author: Dickinson
summary: A psychological lyric on dread and danger as the soul's only stimulus, a fear that spurs it where complacency cannot reach. Themes: fear, the paradoxical vitality of dread, the self under stress.

title: 771. None can experience sting
author: Dickinson
summary: A gnomic lyric on definition by contrast: only those who have known bounty can know want, and poverty requires the memory of wealth. Themes: paradox, privation, knowledge through opposites.

title: 772. The hallowing of Pain
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A lyric on suffering sanctified like heaven, won only at full corporeal cost by those who reach the summit: 'All is the price of All.' Themes: suffering, sanctification through pain, sacrifice, the sublime.

title: 773. Deprived of other Banquet,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wine and Drink · Food and Feasting · The Inn / Tavern
summary: A lyric on feeding the self on scant nutrition that grows sumptuous, sharing a berry like a 'Red Pilgrim' robin. Themes: deprivation, self-sufficiency, humble abundance, charity.

title: 774. It is a lonesome Glee —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the solitary, sanctifying joy of overhearing a distant bird's causeless, sky-borne delight. Themes: joy, solitude, birdsong, transcendence.

title: 776. The Color of a Queen, is this —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric cataloguing a royal color glimpsed in sunset, amber, beryl, and aurora, where nature keeps a rank for witchcraft and iodine. Themes: beauty, color, nature's regal splendor, wonder.

title: 777. The Loneliness One dare not sound —
author: Dickinson
summary: A profound lyric on an unfathomable loneliness, a horror skirted in the dark, whose very scrutiny would destroy the soul that the Maker can illuminate or seal. Themes: loneliness, terror, self and soul, the abyss within.

title: 778. This that would greet — an hour ago —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric on a body that an hour ago would have greeted, now grown to quaint distance, unmoved by Paradise or noon: silver reticence and solid calm. Themes: death, the corpse, transience, the unbridgeable distance of the dead.

title: 779. The Service without Hope —
author: Dickinson
summary: A gnomic lyric praising the tenderest service as that done without hope of reward or goal, a diligence that knows no 'Until.' Themes: selfless devotion, hope, disinterested labor, paradox.

title: 78. A poor — torn heart — a tattered heart —
author: Dickinson
summary: A weary heart taken up by angels and carried to God across the sea of heaven; grief, death and consolation of rest.

title: 780. The Truth — is stirless —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on Truth as an unmoving force that stands without bone or prop even as cedars swerve and mountains lean, holding boldly up all who trust her. Themes: truth, constancy, faith, the immovable.

title: 782. There is an arid Pleasure —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric distinguishing arid pleasure from true joy as frost from dew, one nourishing flowers, the other abhorred. Themes: joy versus its counterfeit, paradox, nature as analogy.

title: 783. The Birds begun at Four o'clock —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A dawn lyric on the immense flood of birdsong at four o'clock, an independent ecstasy of Deity and Men that ends by six, the miracle forgotten as fulfilled. Themes: dawn, birdsong, nature's ecstasy, the sacred ordinary.

title: 784. Bereaved of all, I went abroad —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on inescapable grief personified as a Grave that follows the bereaved everywhere, even abroad, leaving the spade of memory behind. Themes: grief and loss, the grave, memory, the inescapability of mourning.

title: 786. Severer Service of myself
author: Dickinson
summary: A grief lyric on driving the self to exhaustion to fill the vacuum left by a death, finding no drug for consciousness, only death as nature's pharmacy. Themes: grief and loss, affliction, the failure of distraction, mortality.

title: 787. Such is the Force of Happiness —
author: Dickinson
summary: A gnomic lyric contrasting happiness, which lets the least lift a ton, with misery, whose cargo of self is too infinite for slow consciousness to bear. Themes: joy and misery, the weight of suffering, paradox.

title: 788. Joy to have merited the Pain —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric of reunion and devotion: joy to have earned pain in compassing Paradise, and to look again with old eyes upon a beloved face whose haunting will last to eternity. Themes: love, suffering rewarded, memory, immortality of devotion.

title: 789. On a Columnar Self —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on self-reliance and integrity as a granitic, indivisible self that suffices for a crowd, standing with rectitude and God though none be on our side. Themes: self and soul, integrity, self-reliance, faith.

title: 79. Going to Heaven!
author: Dickinson
summary: Astonished, half-skeptical meditation on going to heaven and rejoining the lost dead; faith and doubt over immortality and the grave.

title: 790. Nature — the Gentlest Mother is,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A pastoral lyric personifying Nature as the gentlest mother tending all her children, squirrel, bird, cricket, and flower, then hushing them to sleep with golden lamps. Themes: nature as great mother, providence, tenderness, the natural order.

title: 791. God gave a Loaf to every Bird —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on contentment with a mere crumb that becomes a poignant luxury, making the speaker sovereign over the rich amid imagined famine. Themes: poverty and plenty, contentment, the riches of little, paradox of abundance.

title: 792. Through the strait pass of suffering —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: A devotional lyric on the martyrs treading the strait pass of suffering, faces upon God, faith the everlasting troth like a needle to the north. Themes: martyrdom, faith, suffering, steadfast devotion.

title: 793. Grief is a Mouse —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of riddling definitions personifying grief as mouse, thief, juggler and gourmand, emphasizing its secrecy and refusal to confess even under torture. Explores the concealment and silent endurance of inward suffering.

title: 794. A Drop Fell on the Apple Tree —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A jubilant nature lyric describing a summer rain shower as a festive fete of pearls, jewels and music. Celebrates natural beauty, joy and the renewing exuberance of weather.

title: 795. Her final Summer was it —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy on a woman whose last summer was unrecognized until death made her hurried 'finishing' plain, marked by her Carrara (marble) guide post. Treats mortality, the blindness of the living and seasonal transience.

title: 796. Who Giants know, with lesser Men
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigrammatic meditation on greatness ill at ease in lesser company, contrasted with the unconscious self-sufficiency of a summer gnat. Reflects on greatness, scale and self-perception.

title: 797. By my Window have I for Scenery
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A contemplative lyric on the pine tree seen from her window as an emblem of the divine and immortality, asking whether the dumb can define the divine. Joins nature, faith, immortality and the inexpressibility of the sublime.

title: 798. She staked her Feathers — Gained an Arc —
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird-flight allegory of a soul rising beyond envy into 'Circumference,' at home among the billows of the infinite. Figures aspiration, transcendence and the soul's flight toward immortality.

title: 799. Despair's advantage is achieved
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric arguing that the worth of suffering, despair and death is known only by tasting them oneself. Treats despair, affliction and the epistemology of pain.

title: 8. There is a word
author: Dickinson
cluster: Swords and Weapons · The Battlefield · Horse
summary: A riddle-lyric on the word 'forgot' as a sword that kills the soul; a meditation on memory, oblivion and a kind of spiritual death in war's aftermath.

title: 80. Our lives are Swiss —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Life as cool Switzerland glimpsing forbidden Italy beyond the intervening Alps; longing for a sublime beyond barred by death/limit.

title: 800. Two — were immortal twice —
author: Dickinson
summary: A compressed metaphysical epigram on a privileged few who obtained eternity within time, a 'Reversed Divinity.' Contemplates immortality, paradox and the apprehension of paradise.

title: 801. I play at Riches — to appease
author: Dickinson
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A meditation in which the speaker plays at riches to appease want, prizing poverty's keener appreciation of opulence over actual gold. Explores poverty, desire, want and the paradoxical value of privation.

title: 802. Time feels so vast that were it not
author: Dickinson
summary: A metaphysical epigram fearing that time's vast circumference would engross finitude were it not for eternity, which prepares the soul for a stupendous vision. Sets time against eternity and immortality.

title: 803. Who Court obtain within Himself
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: An aphoristic lyric on inward sovereignty: who holds court within himself sees every man a king, and poverty of monarchy is interior. Treats the self, kingship as metaphor and self-sufficiency.

title: 804. No Notice gave She, but a Change —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy on a woman who died quietly, planted like a seed in fitted ground toward an everlasting spring, declining the mourners' imploring invitation. Joins death, grief, resurrection-hope and seasonal renewal.

title: 805. This Bauble was preferred of Bees —
author: Dickinson
summary: A flower lyric celebrating a blossom prized by bees, butterflies and birds, enamelled by noon, for whom the universe seems made. Treats nature, beauty and flowers as a self-sufficing little world.

title: 806. A Plated Life — diversified
author: Dickinson
summary: A metaphysical epigram in which gold-and-silver pain proves the precious ore within, a value and power that proclaim themselves even as annihilation piles chaos upon them. Treats suffering, endurance and inner worth.

title: 807. Expectation — is Contentment —
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric preferring expectation over satiety, since secure fortune is austere and danger deepens the sum of pleasure. Treats desire, anticipation and the paradox of fulfilment.

title: 81. We should not mind so small a flower —
author: Dickinson
summary: A small flower restores the lost garden and lets faith behold heaven; nature, loss and faith's vision of paradise.

title: 811. The Veins of other Flowers
author: Dickinson
summary: A brief nature lyric on Nature's silent, syllableless creativity, conjugating flowers' veins into 'Branch' and 'Jugular' while she abides and we pass. Treats nature, mortality, transience and the inexpressible.

title: 812. A Light exists in Spring
author: Dickinson
summary: A celebrated lyric on a special light of early spring that science cannot overtake but human nature feels, whose passing is a quality of loss, like trade encroaching on a sacrament. Joins seasons, spring, transience and the sacred in nature.

title: 813. This quiet Dust was Gentleman and Ladies
author: Dickinson
summary: A graveyard epigram noting that quiet dust was once laughter, frocks and curls, a summer's nimble mansion that ceased like bloom and bees. A memento-mori meditation on mortality, dust and transience.

title: 814. One Day is there of the Series
author: Dickinson
summary: A reflective lyric on Thanksgiving Day, dissecting the holiday as a reflex of memory and registering loss — the sharp subtraction of those once present at the table. Joins memory, grief and absence within a New England festival.

title: 815. The Luxury to apprehend
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A love lyric figuring the beloved's countenance as banquet and sumptuous food, the consciousness of 'Thee' the single crumb that feeds plainer days. Treats romantic love, desire and longing through imagery of feasting.

title: 817. Given in Marriage unto Thee
author: Dickinson
summary: A hymn-like lyric on mystical marriage to the Trinity, whose ring alone conquers mortality while earthly betrothals decay. Joins divine love, faith, marriage and immortality.

title: 82. Whose cheek is this?
author: Dickinson
summary: A found flower (a fallen 'pleiad') likened to a dead face covered by robins; nature, death and the indistinct line between cheek and pall.

title: 820. All Circumstances are the Frame
author: Dickinson
summary: A theological epigram in which all circumstances frame God's face, light and dark serve His will, and existence spells out a force illegible. Treats providence, the divine and the inscrutable order of things.

title: 821. Away from Home are some and I —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on being an emigrant away from home in a metropolis of homes, the foreign sky hard to acquire as children's feet retire while their faces remain. Treats exile, home, alienation and childhood.

title: 822. This Consciousness that is aware
author: Dickinson
summary: A major metaphysical lyric on the consciousness that must traverse death alone, the soul condemned to the adventure of its own identity, attended by a single hound. Joins death, identity, the soul and existential solitude.

title: 824. The Wind begun to knead the Grass —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A vivid storm lyric personifying wind, thunder, lightning and rain as a wrecking flood that overlooks the speaker's father's house. Treats nature, storm and providential sparing through dramatic imagery.

title: 827. The Only News I know
author: Dickinson
summary: A hymn-like lyric declaring that the only news, shows and company the speaker knows are immortality, eternity and God along the street of existence. Joins faith, immortality and the eternal as the whole of experience.

title: 828. The Robin is the One
author: Dickinson
summary: A bird lyric celebrating the robin who heralds March and April and submits, speechless from her nest, that home, certainty and sanctity are best. Joins birds, spring, nature and domestic devotion.

title: 829. Ample make this Bed —
author: Dickinson
summary: A solemn elegiac lyric figuring the grave as a bed made with awe, where the dead wait undisturbed till Judgment breaks. Joins death, the grave and resurrection-hope as sleep awaiting the Last Day.

title: 83. Heart, not so heavy as mine
author: Dickinson
summary: A careless street tune heard from a lighter heart soothes the speaker's grief like an anodyne; melancholy, music and consolation.

title: 830. To this World she returned.
author: Dickinson
summary: A compressed lyric of one who returned with a tinge of the other world, half of dust and half of day, like a sod espousing a violet allied chiefly to the skies. Treats immortality, the soul and the union of earthly and heavenly.

title: 831. Dying! To be afraid of thee
author: Dickinson
summary: A martial lyric in which death's artillery is feared only for the friend or beloved it exposes, two armies — Love and Certainty — fighting sternly in a dying eye. Joins death, love, grief and fear through battle imagery.

title: 833. Perhaps you think me stooping
author: Dickinson
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A devotional lyric defending humble stooping by Christ's own example, who stooped until He touched the grave, love annealed and redignified above. Joins divine love, humility, Christ and the Eucharist.

title: 835. Nature and God — I neither knew
author: Dickinson
summary: An epigram in which Nature and God, unknown to the speaker, yet know her like executors of her identity, keeping her secret as secure as Herschel's or Mercury's affairs. Joins faith, nature, identity and the divine gaze.

title: 838. Impossibility, like Wine
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric arguing that impossibility, like wine, exhilarates while possibility is flavorless; a chance's faintest tincture lends enchantment as surely as doom. Treats desire, paradox and the allure of the unattainable.

title: 839. Always Mine!
author: Dickinson
summary: A jubilant lyric of permanent possession, no more vacation, faultless as the rotation of seasons and sun, each dawn first upon God's purple programme. Joins joy, love, dawn and the constancy of grace through seasonal imagery.

title: 84. Her breast is fit for pearls,
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: The humble lover, no diver or crowned suitor, builds a sparrow's nest in the beloved's heart; love, humility and devotion.

title: 840. I cannot buy it — 'tis not sold —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of irreplaceable loss: the speaker's one unbuyable treasure went out the unshut door, leaving her alone and longing only to look it in the eye. Treats grief, loss, longing and the priceless.

title: 842. Good to hide, and hear 'em hunt!
author: Dickinson
summary: A playful epigram on the pleasures of hiding and being found, fox fitting hound, of knowing and telling to the rare, not-too-dull ear. Treats secrecy, concealment and the desire to be understood.

title: 843. I made slow Riches but my Gain
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: An aphoristic lyric on slow, steady riches that increase nightly like the sun, the imperceptible gain inferred less by growing than by the sum it had grown. Treats patience, growth and accumulation through economic metaphor.

title: 846. Twice had Summer her fair Verdure
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric marking two years of summers, winters and autumns to reproach Nature for having no berry for her wandering bird. Joins seasons, nature, grief and the passage of time.

title: 848. Just as He spoke it from his Hands
author: Dickinson
summary: A theological epigram on an edifice (creation/self) as it left the Maker's hands, a turret more or less dishonoring His design, content to ornament His absent character. Treats providence, the divine artificer and design.

title: 85. "They have not chosen me," he said,
author: Dickinson
summary: Christ's broken-hearted statement at Bethlehem; the speaker shares the daisy's dishonor with the rejected Jesus, faith and election.

title: 850. I sing to use the Waiting
author: Dickinson
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A quiet lyric of one who sings to use the waiting, bonnet tied and door shut, until His best step approaches and they journey to the Day. Joins faith, hope, music and song against the dark, and waiting for the beloved or the divine.

title: 851. When the Astronomer stops seeking
author: Dickinson
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A compact lyric arguing that constancy is bedrock: only when astronomer, explorer, and sailor abandon their fixed objects will 'treason' become thinkable, an emblem of unbreakable faith and fidelity.

title: 853. When One has given up One's life
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on renunciation and death likened to sunset, where surrendering life makes lesser losses trivial; a meditation on grief, transience, and the diminishment of regret.

title: 854. Banish Air from Air —
author: Dickinson
summary: A riddling lyric asserting the indivisibility and indestructibility of essential things (air, light, flame, steam) — a near-aphoristic statement of the soul's or love's immortality against human impotence.

title: 855. To own the Art within the Soul
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric praising inner self-sufficiency: to possess the soul's art with silence as company is an inexhaustible estate, a meditation on solitude, the self, and imaginative wealth.

title: 856. There is a finished feeling
author: Dickinson
summary: A graveyard lyric on the strange completed feeling experienced at graves, where death's 'bold Exhibition' clarifies what we are and lets us infer the eternal — mortality and immortality conjoined.

title: 858. This Chasm, Sweet, upon my life
author: Dickinson
summary: An intense lyric addressed to a beloved about a widening chasm/tomb in the speaker's life that she bears like a burial; a meditation on inner despair, death, and love's cost.

title: 861. Split the Lark — and you'll find the Music —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric rebuking the skeptic ('Sceptic Thomas') who would dissect the lark to verify its song — a meditation on faith versus doubt, the violence of analysis, and the truth of inner music.

title: 862. Light is sufficient to itself —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on light's self-sufficiency and impartial generosity — its glow as large to a squirrel in the Himalaya as to us; a meditation on nature, grace, and disinterested abundance.

title: 865. He outstripped Time with but a Bout,
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a soul that outran time, stars, and sun and then contested God at the Throne — a meditation on heroism, immortality, and the contest of the finite with the divine.

title: 867. Escaping backward to perceive
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of being trapped between sea and abyss, retreating up and down as the undermining feet meet — peril at the edge instructs toward the divine; a meditation on terror, the sublime, and revelation.

title: 869. Because the Bee may blameless hum
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of devotion in which the speaker would become bee, flower, or robin to worship the beloved freely — a meditation on love as worship and on nature as the language of adoration.

title: 871. The Sun and Moon must make their haste —
author: Dickinson
summary: A hymnlike lyric in which the Lord's burning glory eclipses sun, moon, and stars, yet He kindles a single candle 'entirely for Thee' — a meditation on divine love, providence, and consolation.

title: 872. As the Starved Maelstrom laps the Navies
author: Dickinson
cluster: Desire · Value and Scarcity · Gems / Jewels
summary: A lyric piling images of devouring hunger — maelstrom, vulture, blood-tasting tiger — to figure the speaker's own 'finer Famine' of desire; a meditation on insatiable longing and appetite.

title: 874. They won't frown always — some sweet Day
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric imagining the speaker's death as the moment when reproving others will relent and seek the child too late — a poignant meditation on death, belated tenderness, and remorse.

title: 875. I stepped from Plank to Plank
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: A famous lyric figuring life as a precarious walk over planks between stars and sea, each step possibly the last — a meditation on uncertainty, peril, and what is called experience.

title: 876. It was a Grave, yet bore no Stone
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on an unmarked grave holding a human soul, whose offence and origin remain unknown until Resurrection — a meditation on death, anonymity, mystery, and the desire to tend the dead.

title: 878. The Sun is gay or stark
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric in which the sun's brightness mirrors and magnifies the mourner's grief, its 'mighty pleasure' adding to our freight — a meditation on grief, nature's indifference, and the burden of bereavement.

title: 879. Each Second is the last
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the drowning man measuring unconsciousness between sea and spar, weighing the terror of failing within a chance against never having had one — a meditation on death, suspense, and risk.

title: 88. As by the dead we love to sit,
author: Dickinson
summary: The dead and the lost grow most dear; grief inflates the value of what is fading in 'broken mathematics.'

title: 880. The Bird must sing to earn the Crumb
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric questioning whether art (the bird's song, the rose's bloom) merits reward when no audience comes — a meditation on the artist, merit, neglect, and self-justifying beauty.

title: 881. I've none to tell me to but Thee
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric of exclusive bond and loss: the speaker has no one but the beloved, whose face has spilled beyond her boundary — a meditation on love, separation, grief, and the longing to overtake the lost.

title: 885. Our little Kinsmen — after Rain
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on earthworms after rain, judged needless until a bird feeds — prompting the analogy 'As I of He, so God of Me'; a meditation on the great chain of being, humility, and divine judgment.

title: 888. When I have seen the Sun emerge
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on the sun's silent daily labor without fame or noise, beside which the earth seems a drum chased by little boys — a meditation on nature, humility, and the vanity of human ambition.

title: 889. Crisis is a Hair
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric figuring crisis as a hair-thin threshold where the least pressure decides life or death and admits eternity — a meditation on mortality, suspense, and the precariousness of being.

title: 89. Some things that fly there be —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Riddle contrasting fleeting things with abiding grief and eternity, and things that rise after rest; transience, mortality and the inexpressible riddle of the skies.

title: 890. From Us She wandered now a Year,
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric on a woman dead a year, her whereabouts unknown in wilderness or ethereal zone — a meditation on death, grief, mystery, and the unseen afterlife.

title: 891. To my quick ear the Leaves — conferred —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric of paranoid exposure in which leaves, bushes, and cave walls become nature's sentinels betraying the hidden speaker — a meditation on surveillance, guilt, and the impossibility of privacy.

title: 892. Who occupies this House?
author: Dickinson
summary: An extended lyric on the graveyard as a 'curious Town' settled before birth, a capital of grave citizens whose owner is a stranger — a meditation on death, the grave, and eternity.

title: 894. Of Consciousness, her awful Mate
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: A lyric on consciousness as the soul's inescapable mate, since nothing can be hidden from God's all-seeing eyes — a meditation on the self, conscience, and divine omniscience.

title: 895. A Cloud withdrew from the Sky
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of regret over a glory glimpsed but not seized, resolving never again to pass an angel with a careless bow — a meditation on lost vision, memory, and aspiration to heaven.

title: 896. Of Silken Speech and Specious Shoe
author: Dickinson
summary: A satiric lyric portraying the bee as a smooth-tongued traitor whose courtship is fickle, pronouncing continual divorce — a meditation on inconstancy, deception, and faithless love.

title: 898. How happy I was if I could forget
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric in which the memory of past 'Bloom' makes present November grief unbearable, leaving the speaker lost like a child perishing of cold — a meditation on memory, grief, and seasonal despair.

title: 9. Through lane it lay — through bramble —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: An allegorical journey poem: children pass through a perilous road of banditti, wolves, serpents and tempests to flutter safely home; life's hazardous pilgrimage.

title: 90. Within my reach!
author: Dickinson
summary: Regret over an unseized chance, figured as unsuspected violets passed an hour too late; missed opportunity, longing and loss.

title: 900. What did They do since I saw Them?
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of eager interrogation of the dead, the speaker refusing to surrender her 'Booty' to God until every question is answered — a meditation on grief, the afterlife, and possessive love.

title: 901. Sweet, to have had them lost
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric ranking the precious dead and those who rose to go yet stayed, finding sweetness in loss reversed to salvation — a meditation on grief, loss, and redemption.

title: 902. The first Day that I was a Life
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric contrasting the first and last day the speaker was 'a Life' — one full, one empty — questioning choice and memory; a meditation on identity, mortality, and self-knowledge.

title: 904. Had I not This, or This, I said,
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: A lyric dialogue with the self on need and deprivation, concluding that hunger persists though the food is gone and that dwelling on loss enfeebles advance — a meditation on want, loss, and endurance.

title: 906. The Admirations — and Contempts — of time —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the 'Compound Vision' of the dying, who through an open tomb see clearly what time obscured — the finite furnished with the infinite; a meditation on death, time, and revelation.

title: 907. Till Death — is narrow Loving —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A lyric arguing that love bounded by death is narrow, while true love so resembles the lost beloved that the lover abdicates self — a meditation on love, grief, self-abnegation, and immortality.

title: 908. 'Tis Sunrise — Little Maid — Hast Thou
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric addressing a 'little Maid' through sunrise, noon, and night who has chosen to die instead of labor — a tender elegy on death, lost industry, and the wish to have dissuaded her.

title: 909. I make His Crescent fill or lack —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: A lyric of mutual mastery between speaker and moon-like beloved, each controlling the other's tides so that neither knows who is despot — a meditation on love, power, and reciprocal dominion.

title: 91. So bashful when I spied her!
author: Dickinson
summary: A shy hidden flower seized blushing and struggling from her haunts; nature, desire and a coy erotic capture kept secret.

title: 910. Experience is the Angled Road
author: Dickinson
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: An aphoristic lyric on experience as a crooked road the mind paradoxically prefers, compelling man to choose his preappointed pain — a meditation on fate, free will, and the discipline of suffering.

title: 911. Too little way the House must lie
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on death's nearness to every heart, whose 'white inhabitant' the soul must emigrate at any moment, losing its neighbor — a meditation on mortality, the soul, and the imminence of death.

title: 93. Went up a year this evening!
author: Dickinson
summary: Anniversary of a quiet death figured as a tranquil tourist ascending from sight; death, memory and serene passage to heaven.

title: 94. Angels, in the early morning
author: Dickinson
summary: A short lyric in which angels are seen gathering dew and flowers at dawn and noon; nature is read as a sacrament tended by heavenly figures, with flowers parching by day.

title: 95. My nosegays are for Captives —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric offering flowers to the captive and dying who wait 'till Paradise'; flowers become a prayer and an errand of consolation toward immortality.

title: 959. A loss of something ever felt I —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on an unnameable primal loss felt since childhood, intuited as a yearning misdirected toward the lost Kingdom of Heaven; meditates on exile, grief, and faith.

title: 96. Sexton! My Master's sleeping here.
author: Dickinson
summary: A graveside lyric in which the speaker tends a beloved's grave, sowing seed and birds' nests so that resurrection-like spring will mark the way; death as sleep and seasonal renewal.

title: 960. As plan for Noon and plan for Night
author: Dickinson
summary: A compressed lyric contrasting Life and Death as differing plans, the foot upon the earth straining toward achievement, the foot upon the grave toward conclusion. Themes of mortality and the soul.

title: 961. Wert Thou but ill — that I might show thee
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A love lyric of self-abnegating devotion, the speaker willing to endure illness, exile, condemnation, and humble service for the beloved, conflating love with religious sacrifice.

title: 962. Midsummer, was it, when They died —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy figuring the dead as a perfected summer harvest, ripened to fullness before the flail of death; merges seasons, fruition, and burial.

title: 963. A nearness to Tremendousness —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of pain that procures nearness to the immense and boundless; affliction locates the soul in illocality, beyond contentment's quiet suburb. Themes of suffering and the sublime.

title: 964. "Unto Me?" I do not know you —
author: Dickinson
summary: A dialogue lyric in which Christ invites the unworthy speaker into Paradise, offering pardon and the chiefest place to the least; dramatizes grace and redemption.

title: 965. Denial — is the only fact
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on the day heaven died, when denial alone is perceived and the earth turns joyless; wisdom is the spoiler of the home. Themes of doubt, grief, and spiritual emptiness.

title: 966. All forgot for recollecting
author: Dickinson
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A love lyric of all-consuming devotion in which home, nature, and self are effaced for a single beloved; the speaker drops her fate like a pebble into his bolder sea.

title: 968. Fitter to see Him, I may be
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of patient waiting to grow worthy through years and seasons to be recognized and chosen by the beloved/divine; gain through loss, beauty through grief.

title: 969. He who in Himself believes —
author: Dickinson
cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: An aphoristic lyric on self-belief and faith as constancy's result, which cannot perish though it fail; meditates on faith, conscience, and integrity.

title: 97. The rainbow never tells me
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A lyric setting nature's wordless evidence (rainbow, flowers, birds) above classical philosophy and Cato; the book of nature outpersuades reasoned argument.

title: 970. Color — Caste — Denomination —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on death's democratic leveling that rubs away the brands of color, caste, and creed, transforming chrysalis to equal butterfly; themes of mortality and equality.

title: 971. Robbed by Death — but that was easy —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric ranking the robberies of death, liberty, distance, and danger, all bounty against the vague calamity of suspense; explores loss, endurance, and dread.

title: 972. Unfulfilled to Observation —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on death as a revolution in locality, incomplete to the eye but a new horizon to faith; suns extinguish here only to dawn opposite. Themes of faith, immortality, and the unseen.

title: 973. 'Twas awkward, but it fitted me —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric on a steadfast old-fashioned heart, faithful as suns and migrating birds, now absent for the technicality of death; merges constancy, love, and mortality.

title: 974. The Soul's distinct connection
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric arguing the soul's link to immortality is best disclosed by danger or calamity, like lightning revealing a hidden landscape; themes of the soul, death, and sudden revelation.

title: 975. The Mountain sat upon the Plain
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A nature lyric personifying the mountain as a watchful patriarch, grandfather of the days and ancestor of dawn, with seasons playing like children at his knees.

title: 976. Death is a Dialogue between
author: Dickinson
summary: A dramatized dialogue between Death and the Spirit, the soul refusing dissolution and laying off the body as an overcoat of clay; dramatizes immortality and the soul-body split.

title: 977. Besides this May
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric of speculation on another May beyond this one, a heavenly spring where saints and the plain neighbor keep eternal season; themes of immortality, faith, and wonder.

title: 978. It bloomed and dropt, a Single Noon —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on a single irreplaceable flower overlooked in passing and never found again; an allegory of unrepeatable beauty, loss, and the regret of inattention.

title: 979. This Merit hath the worst —
author: Dickinson
summary: An aphoristic lyric on the strange relief of the worst, after fate's furthest stone, when the maimed deer no longer attracts the hound; themes of suffering, fate, and endurance.

title: 98. One dignity delays for all —
author: Dickinson
summary: Death imagined as a royal coronation and stately funeral procession that confers rank on all; a memento mori dressed in pomp, purple, and crown.

title: 981. As Sleigh Bells seem in summer
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric on how the absent, once known, become fairy and fictitious, more distant than dawn in Timbuctoo; meditates on absence, memory, and loss.

title: 984. 'Tis Anguish grander than Delight
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric imagining the resurrection-pain of reunion with smitten faces, the wild transport of graves opening and creatures going up two by two; themes of immortality, grief, and faith.

title: 985. The Missing All — prevented Me
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric in which an absolute loss (the Missing All) renders cosmic catastrophe trivial, the speaker unmoved even by a world's departure; explores grief, loss, and numb despair.

title: 986. A narrow fellow in the grass
author: Dickinson
summary: A famous riddling nature lyric describing an encounter with a snake in the grass, evoking nature's kinship yet a chill of dread, zero at the bone.

title: 987. The Leaves like Women interchange
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature · The Book of Nature · The Natural Order
summary: A witty nature lyric personifying leaves as women trading confidences and portentous gossip, sworn to secrecy yet bound to notoriety; light satire of society.

title: 989. Gratitude — is not the mention
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: An aphoristic lyric defining gratitude as silent appreciation beyond speech, like the unsounded depths of the sea; themes of gratitude, the inexpressible, and silence.

title: 99. New feet within my garden go —
author: Dickinson
cluster: Nature vs Civilization · The Garden · Pastoral Retreat
summary: A lyric on the cycle of generations in the garden — new children play above while the weary sleep below — set against the punctual return of spring and snow.

title: 990. Not all die early, dying young —
author: Dickinson
summary: A meditative lyric on the maturity of fate, consummated in a night or in years; it is the act not the period that dies. Themes of mortality, time, and fate.

title: 991. She sped as Petals of a Rose
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy figuring a woman's death as rose-petals scattered by the wind, a frail aristocrat of time leaving a slight default on nature but mountains of grief in the heart.

title: 993. We miss Her, not because We see —
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegiac lyric on missing the dead through the absence of mind, not eye; the departed move like superior stars that still include us. Themes of grief, the soul, and immortality.

title: 995. This was in the White of the Year —
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric contrasting the white (winter) and green (summer) of the year and the difficulty of imagining absent seasons; retrospection becomes half of prospect. Themes of seasons, memory, and time.

title: 997. Crumbling is not an instant's Act
author: Dickinson
summary: A lyric anatomizing ruin as a slow, organized decay of the soul, beginning with a cobweb and rust; the devil's consecutive work. Themes of decay, sin, and mutability.

title: 998. Best Things dwell out of Sight
author: Dickinson
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A compressed aphoristic lyric on hidden value: pearl, the just, and thought dwell out of sight, the best things shunning the public air. Themes of the unseen, truth, and the inexpressible.

title: 999. Superfluous were the Sun
author: Dickinson
summary: An elegy in which the sun is superfluous once excellence is dead, faith just saving the speaker from despair as stars drop anonymous from an abundant sky. Themes of grief, faith, and immortality of fame.

title: A BECK IN WINTER
author: Coleridge
summary: Descriptive fragments of a winter stream and alder, the silent city at midnight, love and hopeless hope; close natural observation merged with reflection on transience.

title: A Boston Ballad (1854)
author: Whitman
summary: A bitter satire on the Fugitive Slave rendition in Boston, summoning Revolutionary ghosts and mockingly crowning King George's skeleton; free-verse on liberty betrayed, ghosts and political critique.

title: A Broadway Pageant
author: Whitman
summary: The Japanese envoys' procession down Broadway becomes a vision of the ancient Orient meeting young America; free-verse on the city, history, and global democratic union.

title: A Carol Closing Sixty-Nine
author: Whitman
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · The First World War · Flags and Banners
summary: A free-verse song of the aged, paralyzed poet still affirming God, freedom, country and faith; themes of old age, mortality, patriotism and faith.

title: A CHARACTER
author: Coleridge
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A self-mocking allegorical satire in which Coleridge figures himself as a maligned bird (Thomas Tit) accused of apostasy, poor and unrewarded. Themes: alienation, the artist and society, satire, integrity.

title: A Child's History of England
author: Dickens
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: Despite the filename, this Markdown contains Dickens's 'The Mudfog and Other Sketches' — comic satirical sketches (Mr. Tulrumble of Mudfog, the Mudfog Association for the Advancement of Everything, The Pantomime of Life). Central matter: satire of provincial officialdom, pseudo-scientific learned societies, and the new railway age, in a parodic-journalistic prose form.

title: A CHILD’S EVENING PRAYER
author: Coleridge
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: Simple hymn-prayer in a child's voice for parents, brothers and an innocent grateful heart, awaking to God's eternal day. Themes of childhood innocence, faith and prayer.

title: A CHRISTMAS CAROL
author: Coleridge
summary: A carol in which the Virgin-Mother, singing over the infant Prince of Peace, denounces war as a murderous fiend and rejoices that the lowly bear the bringer of peace.

title: A Christmas Carol
author: Dickens
cluster: The Supernatural · Terror and Horror · Guilt
summary: A 'Ghost Story of Christmas': the miser Scrooge is visited by Marley's ghost and three Spirits who lead him through past, present and future to moral conversion. Central themes: grace and redemption, charity versus avarice, social injustice and poverty, memory, mortality, set in Victorian London — a redemptive ghostly fable.

title: A Christmas Greeting
author: Whitman
summary: A fraternal greeting to a Brazilian brother nation, affirming the democratic aim and the light of nationhood as more shining than Cross or Crown.

title: A Clear Midnight
author: Whitman
summary: A four-line free-verse lyric of the soul's nocturnal flight toward night, sleep, death and the stars; themes of the soul, night and death.

title: A Cooking Egg
author: Eliot
cluster: Disillusionment · Odysseus / Ulysses · Grace Under Pressure / Stoic Endurance
summary: Ironic quatrain meditation on lost youth, a tepid romance and an imagined heaven of dead worthies; disillusionment, money, the commonplace and the loss of innocence.

title: A DAY-DREAM
author: Coleridge
summary: Tender reverie of love conjured behind closed eyes: fountain, willow, Mary and Asra together. Theme of imagination, memory and domestic love.

title: A Dedication to my Wife
author: Eliot
summary: Intimate love lyric to his wife celebrating shared delight, the breathing of lovers and the rose-garden that is theirs alone.

title: A Descent Into the Maelstrom
author: Poe
summary: A frame-narrative sea tale in which an old fisherman recounts surviving the Norwegian whirlpool by rational observation; explores terror, the sublime, and reason against the destructive power of nature.

title: A DIALOGUE BETWEEN AN AUTHOR AND HIS FRIEND
author: Coleridge
summary: A comic dialogue mocking an author's bad writing, plus epigrams on idle Tom Slothful and on overdressed Bond-street fops; satire of literary vanity and foppery.

title: A DIALOGUE BETWEEN POET AND FRIEND
author: Coleridge
summary: A polemical verse dialogue on church controversy (Milner, Butler, John Huss), with a closing emblem-song of Love as a sword that cuts its own sheath. Themes: faith and doubt, religious controversy, satire, love as war.

title: A Draught of Sunshine
author: Keats
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A bacchic lyric scorning earthly wine for a draught of sunshine and Apollo's inspiration, soaring into an awful poetic ecstasy; wine, inspiration, the god of song and the dread of madness.

title: A Dream
author: Poe
summary: A short early lyric contrasting a cherished 'holy dream' of vanished joy with waking grief; meditates on memory, melancholy, and the light of Truth amid darkness.

title: A DUNGEON
author: Coleridge
summary: A sequence of poetic fragments on confinement, nature, the moon, snow, the grave and madness; imagistic 'studies' for longer poems blending despair and natural description.

title: A Fable for Feasters
author: Eliot
cluster: Wine and Drink · Food and Feasting · The Inn / Tavern
summary: Schoolboy mock-heroic ottava-rima narrative: gluttonous medieval monks feast at Christmas until a ghost carries off the Abbot up the chimney; comic gothic satire of monastic greed.

title: A Farewell to Arms
author: Hemingway
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · The First World War · Flags and Banners
summary: Hemingway's 1929 war novel: Frederic Henry, an American ambulance officer on the Italian front in WWI, deserts after the retreat from Caporetto and flees with Catherine Barkley to Switzerland, where she dies in childbirth — love and disillusionment set against the futility of war.

title: A Florentine Tragedy
author: Wilde
cluster: Justice / Right and Wrong · Revenge · Avenger
summary: Renaissance-Florence blank-verse fragment in which the merchant Simone discovers his wife Bianca with the prince Guido and kills the lover in a duel, ending in jealous, blood-bought desire.

title: A Font of Type
author: Whitman
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: A free-verse metapoetic lyric on the latent power of typeface, the unspoken words slumbering as ocean waves; themes of writing, the book and creative potency.

title: A FRAGMENT FOUND IN A LECTURE-ROOM
author: Coleridge
summary: A satirical fragment depicting Cambridge mathematical study as a dreary bog where the owl Mathesis drives off the Muses and Dulness reigns.

title: A Galloway Song
author: Keats
cluster: Ballad / Ballade · Narrative Poem · The Last Stand
summary: A Scots-dialect ballad-song of a wedding party riding home through the glen while the speaker, left out, sheds sad tears. It pairs a Scottish rural setting, marriage festivity, and grief.

title: A Glimpse
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · The Open Road / Homecoming · The Union
summary: Bar-room vignette of two men content to sit hand in hand amid noise; comradeship, the city, the common man and silent intimacy.

title: A Hand-Mirror
author: Whitman
summary: A stark free-verse confrontation with one's own corrupted body and soul reflected in a mirror; the mirror motif, decay, mortality and self-examination.

title: A HINT TO PREMIERS AND FIRST CONSULS
author: Coleridge
summary: An epigram (from an old tragedy) reminding rulers that power derives from law and that they too must die, paired with a barb on faded beauty; memento mori as political counsel.

title: A HYMN
author: Coleridge
summary: A devotional hymn reading the Creator's power and love in every creature, the book of nature opened to wonder and holy fear. Themes: faith, divine love, wonder and gratitude.

title: A Leaf for Hand in Hand
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · The Open Road / Homecoming · The Union
summary: Offering of a 'leaf' to all natural persons, wishing comrades commonly walk hand in hand; comradeship, leaves, hands, the common man and democracy.

title: A LIAR BY PROFESSION
author: Coleridge
summary: A satirical epigram (after Lessing) on 'Informator', a habitual liar known to lie merely by opening his mouth.

title: A Lover’s Complaint
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Lust / Sexual Desire · Desire · Sin and the Fall
summary: A rhyme-royal narrative complaint in which a forsaken maid, overheard by an aged shepherd, laments her seduction and ruin by a beautiful, deceitful young man; a lyric of unrequited love, deception and faded beauty.

title: A LOVER’S COMPLAINT TO HIS MISTRESS
author: Coleridge
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A reproachful love sonnet to a mistress who deserts the poet to seek a wealthier husband overseas, threatening that the deceitful sea may avenge his grief.

title: (A Lyric): ‘If Time and Space, as Sages say’
author: Eliot
summary: Early carpe-diem lyric: since time and space may be illusory, lovers should pluck the brief flowers of love; meditation on transience and the eternity of a single day.

title: A March in the Ranks Hard-Prest, and the Road Unknown
author: Whitman
cluster: War and its Cost · Blood · American Civil War
summary: A night-march halts at a church turned field-hospital, a scene of blood, surgery and a dying lad; the horror and cost of war witnessed firsthand.

title: A METRICAL ACCIDENT
author: Coleridge
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: A note on casual metre and rhyme found in a prose narrative of Jerome of Prague, who from the flames summons his judges before God; martyrdom rendered as accidental verse.

title: A MIDSUMMER NIGHT’S DREAM
author: Shakespeare
summary: A festive romantic comedy in which four Athenian lovers, a fairy king and queen, and a troupe of rude mechanicals are entangled by love-magic in an enchanted wood; it celebrates imagination, dream, and the irrationality of desire while mocking theatrical illusion.

title: A Noiseless Patient Spider
author: Whitman
summary: Famous two-stanza lyric comparing a spider casting filaments into the void to the soul ceaselessly flinging gossamer threads to connect with the spheres.

title: A Note on War Poetry
author: Eliot
cluster: Nationalism and Patriotism · The First World War · Flags and Banners
summary: WWII meditation on the relation of private experience, war and poetry; reflects on the cost of war and on art transmuting experience into the universal.

title: A Party of Lovers
author: Keats
summary: Comic 'nonsense verses' satirizing love-sick, languid lovers at a tea-party who neglect everything around them; gentle social satire of romantic affectation.

title: A Paumanok Picture
author: Whitman
summary: Imagist seascape of Long Island fishermen drawing a seine of mossbonkers onto the beach; a still, concrete picture of sea and labor.

title: A Persian Lesson
author: Whitman
cluster: Spiritual Emptiness · Eastern Religion / Comparative Religion · Self and Cosmos
summary: A Sufi greybeard in a Persian rose-garden teaches that Allah is immanent in every atom and that the central urge of all things is to return to their divine source.

title: A PLAINTIVE MOVEMENT
author: Coleridge
summary: A plaintive metrical experiment bidding farewell to the pipe, with the moaning wind and an undaisied grave, and notes proposing metre revision; song, loss and prosody.

title: A Prairie Sunset
author: Whitman
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: An imagistic prairie sunset of pure luminous color fighting the silent shadows to the last.

title: A Predicament
author: Poe
cluster: The Grotesque · Good vs Evil · Satanic Figure
summary: A grotesque satire (companion to 'How to Write a Blackwood Article') in which Signora Psyche Zenobia is decapitated by a giant clock-hand; parodies sensational magazine fiction through black comedy and the grotesque.

title: A Promise to California
author: Whitman
cluster: Comradeship · The Open Road / Homecoming · The Union
summary: Promise to travel west to teach 'robust American love'; comradeship bound to westward expansion, the road, and democratic nationhood.

title: A Prophecy: to George Keats in America
author: Keats
cluster: The Poet as Prophet · The Great Mother · The Prophet
summary: A midnight lullaby-prophecy over his brother's unborn child in America, foretelling it will be a poet who grasps the flaming lyre unharmed. It joins poetic vocation, childhood, night and the supernatural.

title: A Riddle Song
author: Whitman
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: A free-verse riddle poem on an ineffable two-word secret pursued by all humanity; themes of inexpressibility, the quest, love and the soul.

title: A Shy Bird
author: Chesterton
summary: A paradoxical familiar essay on English national character, arguing that England's poetry and humour (Shakespeare, Dickens, the common man's songs) hide a shy, soft-hearted, anti-pompous spirit behind a cold reputation; themes of national identity, the common man, nostalgia for Merry England, and the artist and society.

title: A Sight in Camp in the Daybreak Gray and Dim
author: Whitman
cluster: Martyrdom · The Martyr / Saint · The Cross
summary: At dawn the speaker uncovers three dead on stretchers, the last seeming the face of Christ himself; war-death sanctified, the dead soldier as Christ-figure.

title: A SIMILE
author: Coleridge
summary: An extended simile of a shy hind lured by a shepherd's flute, broken off; a delicate fragment of love, music and the tame yet fearful creature drawn by song.

title: A Song About Myself
author: Keats
cluster: Maturation and Growth · Childhood · Innocence and Experience
summary: A comic nonsense song about a 'naughty boy' who runs off to Scotland to scribble poetry and find the north much like home. It is a playful lyric of childhood, wandering, and wonder.

title: A Song for Occupations
author: Whitman
summary: Addressed to workmen and workwomen, asserting the divinity of the common laborer and the soul over institutions; a free-verse catalogue of trades and tools affirming democratic equality.

title: A Song for Simeon
author: Eliot
summary: Aged Simeon's Nunc Dimittis prayer: weariness, death-wind, faith, awaiting salvation, the unspoken Word; memento mori and conversion.

title: A Song of Joys
author: Whitman
summary: An ecstatic free-verse catalogue of the joys of work, the body, the sea, and the senses, culminating in the joy of death and the soul's transcendence of the material.

title: A Song of Opposites
author: Keats
summary: A song embracing joy and sorrow together, weaving paradoxical pairings of mirth and death, roses and serpents; the union of opposites, melancholy and the sweetness of pain.

title: A Song of the Rolling Earth
author: Whitman
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Words are the substantial things of earth and body, not printed signs; a free-verse meditation on nature, the soul, the inexpressible, and the self's own immortality.

title: A STRANGER MINSTREL
author: Coleridge
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A lyric written to the dying Mrs. Robinson, in which the poet on Skiddaw wishes she were present; the personified mountain converses with him, praising her free, immortal poetic spirit.

title: A SUNSET
author: Coleridge
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: Brief nature-lyric describing the sun sinking and vanishing 'as Spirits vanish', a soul-like breeze stirring the wood. Themes of transience, nature and the sublime.

title: A Tale of Jerusalem
author: Poe
summary: A short satirical biblical burlesque in which Jewish priests besieged by Pompey's Romans haul up an unclean hog instead of a sacrificial lamb; a comic clash of religion and mockery during the Roman siege of Jerusalem.

title: A Tale of Two Cities
author: Dickens
cluster: Justice / Right and Wrong · Revenge · Avenger
summary: Dickens's historical novel of London and Paris before and during the French Revolution, tracing resurrection ('Recalled to Life'), class oppression, mob violence, and the self-sacrificial redemption of Sydney Carton, who dies in another's place. Central themes: revolution and its terror, sacrifice, resurrection, social injustice and the cost of violence.

title: A THOUGHT SUGGESTED BY A VIEW OF SADDLEBACK IN CUMBERLAND
author: Coleridge
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: A short nature-lyric on Blencathra's stormy height, contrasting the quiet sublime sky with the noise and riot of earthly things.

title: A TOMBLESS EPITAPH
author: Coleridge
summary: Self-portrait epitaph as 'Satyrane', the studious poet zealous for ancient truth, scorning a hollow age, tracing the springs of Parnassus. Themes of the poet, truth, and contempt for the worldly.

title: A Twilight Song
author: Whitman
cluster: War and its Cost · Blood · American Civil War
summary: By twilight firelight the poet musters the mystic roll of countless unknown Civil War dead, dedicating a special verse to embalm their unwritten names in love.

title: A Valentine
author: Poe
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: An acrostic love poem concealing a lady's name in its lines; a playful puzzle-poem on love, riddle, and the link between names, truth, and poetry.

title: A Voice from Death
author: Whitman
summary: A meditation on a catastrophic flood (Johnstown) as a voice from Death, ministering destruction yet eliciting human sympathy and recalling nature's resistless elemental power.

title: A WISH
author: Coleridge
summary: A blank-verse wish that the poet's life flow gently like a quiet stream, unclogged by wealth and free of glory's bloodstained ambition, ending in a peaceful death.

title: A Woman of No Importance
author: Wilde
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: Wilde's 1893 society comedy turning on the dandy Lord Illingworth, his abandoned former lover Mrs. Arbuthnot and their illegitimate son; an epigram-laden satire of the English aristocracy that exposes the double standard punishing the fallen woman while the man goes free.

title: A Woman Waits for Me
author: Whitman
summary: Frank celebration of sex containing all and of procreation begetting strong future Americans; lust, the body, marriage/procreation, America.

title: a word
author: Chesterton
summary: A narrative lyric tracing the Word (the Christ / Logos born in Galilee) as a star and sword passing through the carpenter's workshop, the fall of Caesars and empires, the age of creeds and crusades, and the industrial age of wheels and smoke, until it resolves into 'Peace'; central concerns are divine love, the ages of the world, and redemption through history.

title: A, B, C
author: Eliot
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: Index-of-first-lines fragment (A–C) for Eliot's collected verse, listing openings such as 'A cold coming we had of it', 'April is the cruellest month' and 'Among the smoke and fog'; an apparatus pointing to the whole corpus.

title: a-hymn
author: Chesterton
cluster: Grace and Redemption · Humility · The Desert
summary: A national hymn and prayer (three stanzas, hymn-meter) begging God to take away the people's pride and to deliver a corrupt, gold-walled nation from lies, profit and damnation; central themes are faith, national renewal, humility, and the corruption of power.

title: Aboard at a Ship’s Helm
author: Whitman
summary: A warning bell saves a ship from wreck, opening into the ship of body and soul voyaging on; free-verse lyric on the sea, ships, the journey and the soul.

title: Abou ben Adhem
author: Chesterton
summary: A satirical parody of Leigh Hunt's 'Abou Ben Adhem', in heroic couplets, in which the secular philanthropist who loves his fellow-men but not God reveals himself as a tyrannical social engineer; central themes are satire of society, secular humanism vs faith, and the loss of wonder.

title: ABSENCE: A FAREWELL ODE ON QUITTING SCHOOL FOR JESUS COLLEGE, CAMBRIDGE
author: Coleridge
summary: A farewell ode on departing for Cambridge, lamenting lost days of peace and Eden-like innocence yet consoling itself that absence, like the moon's return, will renew delight.

title: Acrostic
author: Keats
summary: An acrostic on Georgiana Augusta Keats invoking Apollo and the Muses, valuing love and brotherhood above mastery of verse. It joins poetic inspiration, family affection, and friendship.

title: AD LYRAM.
author: Coleridge
summary: Latin original (after Casimir) of the lyre poem: hang up the lyre, recline by the bank, while clouds gather and joys flee on fleeting foot; on transience and the lyre.

title: AD VILMUM AXIOLOGUM
author: Coleridge
cluster: The Poet as Prophet · The Great Mother · The Prophet
summary: Hexameter address to Wordsworth, hymning his song as a divine, immortal word, love the spirit of life and music the life of the spirit. The poet as prophet.

title: ADAPTATIONS
author: Coleridge
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: An editorial note on Coleridge's adaptations and 'garblings' of seventeenth-century poets used as mottoes in the Biographia and The Friend, listing three adapted poems; intertextual borrowing and literary criticism.

title: ADDRESSED TO A YOUNG MAN OF FORTUNE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A reproachful sonnet-like address rebuking C. Lloyd's self-indulgent melancholy by confronting him with real poverty, war and social injustice, urging active sympathy for mankind.

title: ADDRESSED TO HAYDON
author: Keats
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: Sonnet praising disinterested 'singleness of aim' and the steadfast genius who defies envy and a money-mongering world; the artist against society.

title: ADDRESSED TO THE SAME
author: Keats
cluster: The Poet as Prophet · The Great Mother · The Prophet
summary: Sonnet hailing the great living spirits (Wordsworth, Hunt, Haydon) as prophets of a coming age; the poet as prophet, artistic vocation and a new dawn.

title: Adieu to a Soldier
author: Whitman
cluster: The Road · Napoleonic Wars / the Navy
summary: Farewell to a comrade-soldier whose mission is fulfilled while the poet marches on to fiercer spiritual battles; comradeship, war, and the road of struggle.

title: After the Dazzle of Day
author: Whitman
summary: Short lyric: only after day's dazzle and clangor fade do stars and the true inner symphony emerge.

title: After the Sea-Ship
author: Whitman
summary: The wake of a sea-ship and its frolicking procession of waves; a sensuous free-verse lyric on the sea, ships, water and motion.

title: After the Supper and Talk
author: Whitman
summary: A meditation on death as the lingering, reluctant final farewell of a friend departing into darkness on a journey of no return.

title: Ages and Ages Returning at Intervals
author: Whitman
summary: The phallic, immortal chanter of Adamic songs returning through ages, bathing his songs in sex; eternal return, the body, lust, immortality.

title: Agnes Grey
author: Bronte
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: Anne Bronte's 1847 first-person novel of a poor clergyman's daughter who becomes a governess, enduring the cruelty and snobbery of her employers before finding love and a quiet pious marriage; a realist social novel on the dignity of work, faith and moral integrity.

title: Ah Poverties, Wincings, and Sulky Retreats
author: Whitman
summary: A free-verse lyric figuring life as a war against inner foes that the true self will overcome; themes of the self and soul, struggle and ultimate victory.

title: Al Aaraaf
author: Poe
summary: A long, allusive cosmic poem set on Tycho Brahe's wandering star, an afterworld of pure Beauty where the angel Nesace and lovers Angelo and Ianthe dwell; explores beauty, knowledge, death, and the gulf between earthly and ideal.

title: alarms and discursions
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: A 1911 collection of whimsical familiar essays built on paradox, defending the ordinary, the English countryside and 'Merry England' against industrialism, plutocracy and the cult of progress, with recurrent imagery of grey weather, gargoyles, and the legend of King Alfred at Ethandune; central concerns are anti-industrialism, paradox, the common man, and the critique of progress.

title: ALCAEUS TO SAPPHO
author: Coleridge
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: A classicizing love-lyric in the voice of Alcaeus praising the blush, eyes and lip of his beloved Sappho as the fairest face on earth.

title: ALICE DU CLOS OR THE FORKED TONGUE
author: Coleridge
cluster: Ballad / Ballade · Narrative Poem · The Last Stand
summary: A medieval ballad in which the vassal Sir Hugh's double-tongued slander goads jealous Lord Julian into killing his innocent betrothed Alice with an arrow. Themes: deception, jealousy, betrayal, innocence destroyed.

title: All I Survey
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: A 1933 collection of Chesterton's familiar essays ranging over childhood, literary criticism (Swift, Gray, Scott, Chaucer), industrialism, education, war memorials and modern paganism. Central matter: defence of common sense and tradition, satire of fashionable progress, and the critique of industrial society.

title: ALL IS TRUE - (HENRY VIII)
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Power and Corruption · The Crown · Pride
summary: A late history play (with Fletcher) dramatizing the fall of Buckingham, Wolsey's rise and disgrace, Katherine's repudiation and Anne Boleyn's rise toward Elizabeth's birth; themes are the falls of the great, power and ambition, conscience, and providential history.

title: All Is Truth
author: Whitman
cluster: Spiritual Emptiness · Eastern Religion / Comparative Religion · Self and Cosmos
summary: A meditative free-verse lyric affirming that all things, even apparent lies, partake of universal truth; themes of truth, identity and the self and cosmos.

title: ALLA SUA AMICA
author: Coleridge
cluster: Lust / Sexual Desire · Desire · Sin and the Fall
summary: Marino's Italian sonnet: two guilty lovers, condemned to death and to hell, find their eternal fire in each other's heart and eyes; a Baroque sonnet of guilty love, sin, damnation and fire (with an appended German love-fragment).

title: ALLEGORIC VISION
author: Coleridge
summary: A prose dream-allegory: a pilgrim's vision of the Valley of Life, the Temple of Superstition, the matron Religion, and the cave of Blasphemy and atheism that proves Janus-faced with Superstition; faith, doubt and true religion.

title: alliterativism
author: Chesterton
summary: A 1914 comic light-verse squib mocking, through relentless alliteration, the wartime newspaper rhetoric about 'violating Belgian neutrality'. A satirical patriotic parody touching on the First World War.

title: AllThingsConsidered-8
author: Chesterton
summary: Chesterton's 1908 collection of journalistic familiar essays (the ephemeral, the fallacy of success, patriotism and sport, two cities, Oxford). Central matter: defence of common sense and morality against modern fashions, satire of journalism and society, paradox.

title: ALL’S WELL THAT ENDS WELL
author: Shakespeare
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: A Jacobean 'problem play' comedy in which Helen, a physician's daughter, wins the reluctant aristocrat Bertram through a cure, an enforced marriage and the bed-trick; central themes are unrequited love, class disparity, virtue versus rank, and an uneasily happy resolution.

title: Alone
author: Poe
cluster: Wonder and Gratitude · The Sublime · Sun
summary: An early confessional lyric on the poet's lifelong sense of difference and isolation from childhood; themes of alienation, melancholy, and a visionary apartness drawn from nature's storms.

title: Also by T. S. Eliot
author: Eliot
cluster: The Artist and Society · The Book / Reading · Clothing and Costume
summary: Back-matter bibliography listing Eliot's collected poems, Four Quartets, the plays, literary and social criticism, plus the ebook copyright page; an editorial/bibliographic apparatus to the corpus.

title: ALWAYS AUDIBLE
author: Coleridge
summary: A short satirical epigram on drunken 'Jack', roaring at midnight and snoring at noon, mocking drink and idleness.

title: america
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: Essay from What I Saw in America (1922) arguing that America is the only nation founded on a creed (the Declaration of Independence). Themes: nationhood, travel and the foreigner, the contrast of English character with American dogma, satire of officialism.

title: America
author: Whitman
summary: Personifies America as an enduring towering Mother of equality, freedom and law, a patriotic celebration.

title: American Fundamentalists
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: 1925 essay on the Scopes 'Monkey Trial' defending tradition and Fundamentalism's instinct against fashionable Darwinism, built around the meaning of paradox. Themes: faith and doubt, critique of progress, tradition, satire.

title: American Notes
author: Dickens
cluster: The Journey · The Quest · The Pilgrim
summary: Dickens's travel book recording his 1842 journey through the United States (and, in this edition, Pictures from Italy), observing American institutions, prisons, factory life, and above all delivering a sustained indictment of slavery. Central matter: travel writing as social observation and reformist satire of institutions, with a strong moral critique of slavery and social injustice.

title: american-morals
author: Chesterton
cluster: Essay · Critique of Progress · The Common Man
summary: Essay attacking the confused American 'standard of right and wrong' (the prohibitionist horror of tobacco) as the decay of Puritanism into formless fanaticism. Themes: justice/morality, satire of society, critique of Puritanism.

title: americanisation
author: Chesterton
summary: Satirical patriotic poem resisting the Americanisation of British life ('Britannia needs no Boulevards'), invoking the Dance of Death and a declaration of independence. Themes: nationalism, satire of society, critique of progress.

title: Among the Multitude
author: Whitman
cluster: Romantic Love · The Lover · Unrequited / Frustrated Love
summary: Within the crowd one 'lover and perfect equal' picks out the poet by secret signs; love, identity, the city and mutual recognition.

title: AN ANGEL VISITANT
author: Coleridge
summary: Brief lyric fragment of a warm, still bower where the lovers are together and the heart stays glad through tears. Themes of love, nature and momentary bliss.

title: AN APOLOGY FOR SPENCERS
author: Coleridge
summary: A satirical dialogue epigram joking that the poor buy half-coats (spencers) because they cannot afford whole ones, glancing at poverty.

title: An Army Corps on the March
author: Whitman
cluster: Swords and Weapons · The Battlefield · Horse
summary: A compact battlefield image of dust-covered ranks and rumbling artillery pressing on under the sun; the relentless mass-motion of an army.

title: An Enigma
author: Poe
cluster: Letters and Writing · Immortality Through Verse · Immortality of Art / Fame
summary: A sonnet that both mocks shallow sonnets and conceals a lady's name acrostically; reflects on transience, immortality through naming, and the craft of the poetic riddle.

title: AN EXPERIMENT FOR A METRE
author: Coleridge
summary: A metrical experiment (scanned) praising a beauty bright as an angel that dazzles and awes; prosodic study in a love-compliment lyric.

title: An Extempore
author: Keats
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
summary: An extempore comic narrative of a wilful princess and her transformed servants (dwarf, ape, fool) at an empty faery court, with a sly moral on beauty and folly. It is a playful fairy-tale satire of vanity and transformation in an enchanted wood.

title: An Ideal Husband
author: Wilde
cluster: Money and Gold · Marriage and Fidelity · Social Injustice
